en: *Commentary on the Chapter on Manifest and Non-manifest*:
Regarding the "Chapter on Manifest and Non-manifest," there are two explanations for the terms "manifest" (*vijñapti*) and "non-manifest" (*avijñapti*), as follows.

As for the phrase "if there is that which one does not wish, etc.," this refers to that which is not concomitant with body and speech; [whereas] that which is concomitant with body and speech is the characteristic [of the manifest].

Because it is difficult to know. Question: Are there only three types of volition (*cetanā*) expressed by the mind? Answer: Yes. For example, one who wishes to cultivate the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) first deliberates upon what is appropriate and what is not.
One considers when and where one should maintain upright tranquility and meditative concentration;

this mental activity is called "deliberative volition" (*tulanā-cetanā*). Having completed this deliberation and known what is suitable, one then determines the specific point of action; this is [the volition of] "decision."
When the resolve is fixed and can no longer be altered, it is called "decisive volition" (*niyata-cetanā*).

Subsequently, when one sits alone in a quiet place at the appropriate time and location, contemplating sentient beings who suffer with the thought of freeing them from suffering, and contemplating those who lack happiness with the thought of bestowing happiness upon them—such instances as these are called "impelling volition" (*preraka-cetanā*).
Because it involves the intention to act, that which precedes the preparatory stage (*prayoga*)—when correct conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) has not yet arisen—is not called the "fundamental" (*maula*).

In this way, the three types of volitional action (*cetanā-karmapatha*) are also established. Question: What are the characteristics of those [actions] belonging solely to body and speech, as well as those associated with all three?

Since body and speech must necessarily be prompted by the mind, how are they defined? Answer: When one first generates a sincere mind and then performs physical prostrations or verbal praise, although these are prompted by the mind, they are nonetheless designated as [the paths of action].

Second, regarding karma: when one arouses the mind and, upon reaching the [meditative] time, applies oneself with single-minded devotion, exerting the body and purifying speech while also exerting the mind to contemplate the form of the image—this is called the movement and arousal of the three types of karma.
This is because, from the point of the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) onward, they become distinct.
Regarding the phrase "this meaning indicates," etc.: this first master distinguishes that among the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), only the wholesome (*kuśala*) gives rise to it.

As for the statement "giving rise to the unmanifest without intention," the character "intention" (*yi*) appears to be superfluous; however, according to the logic of the text, it serves to exclude cases where only the non-manifest arises.
Others add the character "intentional" (*manas*) [to the term]. It is only that which arises from non-intentional expression (*avyākṛta*) that is called "non-manifest" (*avijñapti*). Question:

Since all seeds (*bīja*) are likewise non-intentionally known, on what basis is "non-manifest" specifically distinguished? Answer: It is only that which increases (*vṛddhi*) that is called "non-manifest.
That which does not increase, even if it is not intentionally known by itself, is not called "non-manifest. Why is this so? Because...

That which possesses superior capacity yet is not clearly cognized is established as the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). If it is something generally unknown, what is the need for its separate establishment?

It is like a person of worldly excellence whose reputation is not manifest; because everyone shares this understanding, they are called a "recluse" (*śramaṇa*). What need is there to mention others who have no name?
As for the statement that [the unmanifest] is also accomplished by Bodhisattvas, it certainly does not exist for those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Section. Regarding "there being only three branches": non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion constitute the three. Section.
Regarding "the remaining defiled and neutral": the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*)—namely, the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured (*nivṛta*)—are both termed "defiled.
Elsewhere, if it says "unwholesome and neutral," the term "neutral" therein includes the obscured as well.
Regarding the phrase "the predominance of karma" and so forth: this is also the same as the seven branches [of the path], which arise only when they are of the superior grade;
those of the middling or inferior grades do not. Some say that the intermediate grade constitutes the inferior grade; this is stated from a specific perspective.
If it were truly the inferior grade, one would know it to be otherwise, because it must necessarily include the intermediate grade here, as indicated by the *Yideng* (The Lamp of Meaning).
Section. Regarding the statement "there is an interpretation that [it is] unwholesome, etc.": this is the second explanation, wherein both natures (wholesome and unwholesome) give rise to it.

Section. Regarding the statement "the ten unwholesome paths of action": since the latter three mental actions constitute a *pārājika* offense, how is it that they do not give rise to a distinct, superior non-informative (*avijñapti*) karma?
[Chapter]. "Is it not merely that volitions (cetanā) of body and speech plant [seeds]?

Below this, he again provides two examples of the characteristics of karma, stating that volitions of the mind alone [plant seeds], while the other two [of body and speech] are both productive. Master Zhou calls the wholesome and the unwholesome "the two.
Now, against whom is this statement directed? The former master has already stated that the wholesome is what initiates [action]. Furthermore, some say that the unwholesome does not...

To claim that there are two types of "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) based on their names is a somewhat erroneous statement; for this master does not hold that unmanifest karma can be produced by the mind alone. My current interpretation of this point is as follows:
what is referred to as "two" refers to their distinct natures (*bhinnārtha*), meaning they are different from the bodily and vocal [actions] which are designated as "two.

Alternatively, this may refer to the principle of the ten successive layers (*daśa-koṭi*). Why is this so? For how could it be that only bodily and vocal actions constitute multiple layers of unmanifest karma, while the mental alone does not?
If they were different, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) would not be established. Question: Why are these two [terms] synonymous? Answer:
Because "this" and "that" are not the same, how could they not be two? There is a common worldly expression: those who look well upon one another say, "There is no duality."

Section. Regarding the three types of punitive karma (*daṇḍakarma*): the three—body, speech, and mind—restrain sentient beings; these are called the three types of punitive karma. Furthermore, upon examining the explicit text: Section.
As for "the mental non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*), etc.," because this is merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), it is not mentioned here; that treatise states that it does not exist.
"Because it is manifest form.

Chapter. Regarding the statement "some maintain that intention manifests [the precept]," this refers to the third master. He maintains that nothing is ever initiated; first through instruction and subsequently through principle.
Since his principle holds that the great intent does not externally manifest to others, it is not of the superior grade, and therefore there is no non-manifest (avijñapti) form.

Section: Regarding the phrase "although it mentions the ten wholesome [actions]," etc., this is in response to the potential objection: "When you speak of the ten wholesome precepts (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*), do you not mean the three types of mental action?

This is answered by explaining that the name "ten wholesome precepts" is designated based on the predominant factor (*adhikāra*). Here, "karma" (action) is broad while "precept" (restraint) is narrow.

Chapter. Regarding the various [positions] among these two theories, they speak of three masters. This is because the first two masters are combined as they agree in asserting that [the seeds] are produced.

Now, in explaining this statement, although there are three masters, for both the wholesome and the unwholesome, each maintains only two positions regarding whether [seeds] are produced or not produced. The *Dīpa* (Lamp) states in its second section:
"The *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) records two theories; one may use them as one pleases, but the latter theory is taken as definitive. Now, here...

It is established by principle that the non-informative (avijñapti) arises from the intention; since the Bodhisattva precepts fully restrain the three types of action and are superior to those of the two vehicles, extending to the end of the future, how could they not give rise to a particularly sublime non-informative?
The first two explanations are based on the intermediate state and do not refer to the formal discipline (saṃvara).

This statement prior [to the distinction] is identical to what follows; although there is dispute regarding whether it is discipline or non-discipline in the intermediate state, the non-informative definitely arises.
The unmanifest (*avijñapti*) cannot be contested. Question: What is the difference between these [two] preceding and following [explanations]? Answer:

This [section] distinguishes the gateway through which the three types of karma are initiated; below, it distinguishes the number of categories within the essence of the unmanifest. Furthermore, there are two masters. Although the masters do not differ, there are distinctions in their thematic approaches.
All masters maintain that the initiator is primary; this applies to both natures, and likewise to those who hold a middle position.
Regarding the *Abhidharma* and the *Vijñaptimātra*, they establish [the unmanifest] as "matter" (*rūpa*) by way of its commonality across the three vehicles;
therefore, there is no contradiction. In the section on "unmanifest matter," this constitutes the first interpretation, wherein the unmanifest possesses all three [aspects].

Under the section beginning with "There is another view," it is the second interpretation, wherein the unmanifest possesses only two. Question: In what follows, should there not be the three mental [actions]? Answer: [It is so.]

The heading is narrow while the explanation is broad. The heading follows the various teachings by mentioning only its color, whereas the explanation exhausts the principle by encompassing all ten members (*daśāṅga*).

Alternatively, the phrase "only the color of the ten members" below provides a brief indication according to the teaching. Furthermore, the intention regarding the arising [of the members] has already been debated within the preceding table.

This clearly demonstrates whether the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) exists or not; thus, it merely indicates the unmanifest form (*rūpa*). Only when the preceding and succeeding passages mutually clarify one another is the text complete. Question:

Why were these three [aspects] not included in the discussion of the manifest (*vijñapti*) that preceded this? Answer: Because the maintenance of vows and their transgression reside precisely in the state of the unmanifest;
since the manifest is extremely brief in duration, how could it serve as the basis for the Vinaya and other codes?

Section. Regarding "if one performs acts such as giving" and so forth: that which is wholesome yet not a formal vow (*saṃvara*), or unwholesome yet not a non-vow (*asaṃvara*), is termed "intermediate" (*madhyastha*).
It is not of a single nature. One should know from the following text that there is only the interpretation of it being of a single nature, as will be explained below.

Since this is also called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*), it must necessarily involve a specific intention or aspiration; it is not merely performing acts such as giving in a general or casual manner that is so named.

It is situated in the middle, because in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, both the disciplined (*saṃvara*) and undisciplined (*asaṃvara*) are explained in the same section. Thus, that treatise states:

"However, based on volition and aspiration... [it] is established as being either based on the stage where the seeds of wholesome or unwholesome volitions that initiate superior bodily and vocal actions increase."
In this context, because the seven meanings are not differentiated, the "pivot" (kṣura) precedes and the "lamp" (pradīpa) follows, which is said to apply generally to the intermediate stage;

thus, it also constitutes the limit of the superior grade of aspiration. As for the statement in the *Zǎn* that this is of the inferior grade, this refers to its specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in that it does not aspire to livelihood.

That which has not yet entered the legal code is called "inferior grade" (*hīna*). It is not by reference to the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) that it is called inferior grade;

therefore, the locus of the arousal of the thought must necessarily be of "superior grade" (*adhimātra*). Otherwise, there would be no principle for its progressive increase. That which does not undergo progressive increase is not termed "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).

Question: If this is so, what is the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) of this? Answer: For now, regarding the vows of restraint (*saṃvara*), there are only seven classes of practitioners (*saptanikāya*). As for their branches (*aṅga*)...

Because the divisions and limits must not be lacking, and because legal codes and ritual protocols are no different in this regard. Such instances where the time for receiving [the precepts] is short and so forth are all termed "intermediate" (*madhya*).

There is a clear textual authority for this in the twelfth fascicle of the *Za* (Compendium). Below, in the analysis of abandoning the intermediate state within the community, it includes the precept of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*).
Since the intermediate state is contained within the gathering of virtuous qualities, it is for this reason that the term "laying out" (*prajñapti*) is now mentioned.

[This refers to] the giving [of precepts] and so forth. Question: Among *upāsakas* and *upāsikās*, there is the practice of receiving [precepts] with partial observance (*aṃśika*). Why are they not included among the seven classes of followers? Answer:

Because when one is categorized within those [seven], such a case constitutes being "intermediate" (*madhyama*). This is because, according to their type, they may either observe the precepts in full or only partially.

The *Zuǎnshū* (Compendium of Commentaries) also states that within the *bhikṣu* precepts, observing them for a short duration is termed "intermediate. As for "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*), which is the opposite of "restraint" (*saṃvara*), it must necessarily involve [the intention to] live [by means of harming others].
Because that which constitutes livelihood is [only] action; the other [acts], such as killing and so forth, are not considered livelihood. That which sustains life is called "abiding in the middle.
Similarly, the mention here of "beating and so forth" also refers to those instances where there is a deliberate intention and a fixed limit.

Question: How can the principle of sustaining life be the opposite of ethical discipline (*saṃvara*)? Answer: All forms of ethical discipline are called "the path of livelihood" because they are the means by which one lives. As it is said: [like...]

The *Zuǎn* (Compendium) also has some minor omissions from its early period; however, these are not of another kind. Those that briefly synthesize the various sections are all termed "intermediate" (*chùzhōng*).
*Ōu* means to strike; thus, both the name and its definition are clearly manifested.

Section: Regarding "Decisive Determination" (*viniścaya*) and so forth: following the previous reiteration of the section on non-informative action (*avijñapti*), this section establishes the position of the later master as distinct from the preceding one.

While the former portion analyzed the essential nature and characteristics, the present portion cites scriptural authority. In the fifty-third [chapter], which correctly explains the intermediate [course of action], the two excluded [factors] possess all ten branches.
As for the term "all," it refers to those who possess a formal vow; among them, it applies to all cases of the highest degree.
It is not merely a matter of general good and evil.

Regarding the fifty-fourth section on "the three [types of] speech" and so forth: although the text speaks of the three as being the "middle," it states that their color and function must certainly not be those of the three mental [factors].

Section. Regarding the statement that there are [karmas] such as giving (*dāna*), since their essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are already observed and the scriptural texts (*śāstra*) are also clear, it follows that intermediate karma (*madhyama-karman*) also possesses non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

Section. Regarding the interpretation that "intermediate [karma] exists," this master also adheres to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), maintaining that it must be of superior grade (*adhimātra*) [to constitute non-informative matter].
[The text] states: "It accomplishes the non-informative (*avijñapti*). Since this [state] is not superior, there is no non-informative [action].

Regarding the phrase "this is also not so," etc., the following passage raises an objection; it summarizes the general meaning of the previous difficulty and the subsequent master’s position. [The opponent argues:

"If one establishes the non-informative for those who abide in the intermediate state as being of the lowest-of-the-low grade, while this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) extends to the higher [grades], it contradicts that [position]. Question: How can there be restraint (*saṃvara*)?
[Objection: This contradicts the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, for it relies on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. [Response: Within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, there are broadly three grades;

their superiority and inferiority are as described. However, here we are considering the infinite internal sub-classifications. Thus, even within the superior grade, we discuss them in further detail.

This does not preclude the fact that the restraint (*saṃvara*) of the intermediate category is inferior to that of the full category; rather, it is simply a matter of the completeness or deficiency of its constituent branches and time periods. It is not [a contradiction].

Regarding the classification into two types based on the generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), the present [category] lacks its constituent factors; however, why should this invalidate the generation of the mind and the request for the reception of the superior ordination (*viśeṣa-saṃvara*) at that time?
For such cases exist regarding the practice of giving (*dāna*) and so forth. Question: Within this context, why is it said that "thought" (*cetanā*) is specifically termed "superior"?

What constitutes the excellence of these physical manifestations? Answer: To apply oneself with earnestness through the three karmas (of body, speech, and mind) to the utmost extent of one's capacity is called "excellent.
It is not necessary for tears to flow profusely, blood to issue from the face, or the hair on the body to stand on end to be called "middling."

Regarding the passage beginning with "Although it is said that the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) is equal," the character *fǎ* (dharma) in the *Jíxuán* (Compendium of Mysteries) has been changed to *zhū* (all/various).

Below this, the contradictions are reconciled: first the [contradictory] statements are cited, and then they are harmonized. This precisely concerns the division within the proximate objects of the homogeneous reception (*sabhāga*). If divided according to categories, they are three;
if discussed in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), they are internal. Whether three or two, there is no contradiction between them.

Section. Regarding the phrase "in all cases it is intermediate": hereafter, the latter master raises an objection against the former master. Since it is said to be "intermediate," how could there be a "superior" grade?
Therefore, there is no unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*).

Regarding the phrase "among the two explanations," although these words exist, the former interpretation is correct, as it accords with the majority of the teachings and is more consistent with reason.

By analogy, "indicating" (*vijñapti*)—as intended by the previous discussion—is also a "middle" [position]. Thus, there has never been any dispute regarding the formal restraint (*saṃvara*) or non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) of these three types of action;
the two views differ only concerning the "middle" position. The preceding section analyzed the indicative manifestation of the mind.

Whether [the non-manifesting action] arises or not, it corresponds to the presence or absence of the non-manifesting action within the mind. Here, the discussion concerns whether the non-manifesting action exists within the body and speech during acts such as giving and so forth;
it is also observed that the two types of manifesting actions (bodily and vocal) either arise or do not arise.

Previously, there was no dispute regarding the body and speech, and here, there has been no analysis of the mind; thus, the meaning of the text is already sufficient through the mutual clarification of both aspects. If...
To describe them all in detail would result in excessive prolixity.
Regarding the statement that "the sense faculties, the primary elements, and derived matter" are so: the first four phrases provide a general explanation of their essential nature as a whole;

the subsequent three phrases further specify them. The former constitutes three categories and the latter two pairs; their intrinsic natures are no different. [This refers to] the five sense faculties.
It is one. The primary elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute one, and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) constitutes another. Derived matter refers to the four sense objects (*viṣaya*).

These, together with the five faculties (*indriya*), are collectively termed "derived" (*upādāya*), while the primary elements are what "produce" them. Thus, the faculties are combined and established under a single name.

Below this, although [the text] alternates between granting and refuting [the opponent's view], it essentially requires a distinct body; because it manifests by relying upon this, it is called the "body of reliance" (*āśraya-kāya*), rather than being an establishment [of a separate entity]. Question: As for...

Why is it that the individual sense-faculties (*indriya*) receive a collective name? Answer: Because this [body] is the basis; because the multitude gathers here, it receives this name, while for the others, no such designation is established.
Regarding the passage "Furthermore, in the sense of being a support," etc.: this second meaning further possesses the nature of being a "body" (*kāya*) as a single entity. This...
[The rest] is omitted.
Regarding the phrase "and many dharmas," this also serves as a general rebuttal. An external opponent should ask:

"If the meaning of 'body' (*kāya*) is defined as 'that which serves as a basis,' then would not the sense organs such as the eye also be so? To answer this, it is said: "They do not serve as [a basis] for many."

Because it serves as a basis; this [consciousness] takes the eye and so forth as its basis up to that point, and each of those [senses] serves as the basis for the consciousness of its own respective object.
Since it is not the case for all [objects], it does not receive that name.
Regarding the phrase "manifestation means to indicate, etc.": the action of bodily manifestation has only one meaning, whereas the manifestation of speech has two meanings.
By adding the character *zì* (self) above the character *nèi* (internal), the meaning becomes clear upon reading it.

Section: Regarding "that which depends on the body as its manifestation" (kāyavijñapti): The body is the body-faculty (kāyendriya) and does not manifest the internal mind itself; rather, it takes up forms such as the bending and stretching that depend upon the body to represent the internal mind.
Therefore, this is an *adhikaraṇasādhana* (locative determinative compound). This differs from vocal manifestation (vāgvijñapti), for speech can reveal the mind so that others may know it;
thus, the latter is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative compound).

Section. Regarding the distinction between the two interpretations of the phrase "this can manifest" (*abhivyañjaka*), etc.: In the former interpretation, the term "manifest" (*abhivyakti*) does not refer to the signified object (*vācya*), but is defined directly as the manifestation within the internal mind.
In the latter interpretation, the term "manifest" refers to the signified object; it is defined as the process of signifying and manifesting that extends from the object back toward the mind.
Therefore, they are different. Question: The former interpretation may be acceptable, but how can the latter be called "informative action" (*vijñapti-karman*)?
In this context, the primary purpose is to represent the internal state so that others may know it. The answer is:

one must also cause others to know what one intends to say, because raising [the speech] serves as a medium of expression that can be shown to others. Alternatively, these two meanings must be combined to be complete, as they express both the speaker and the subject matter spoken about.
Some say that both interpretations are valid; however, taking the conventional sound [of the term], the former interpretation is not [correct].

To claim that the later explanation includes both the name and the object, and thus differs from the former, is incorrect. Now, it is held that one must certainly take the actual sound (*dhvani*), for it is only by causing another to hear it that one expresses oneself;
therefore, there is no fault in subsuming the provisional under the real, as in the case of names and so forth. This is not the case with isolated function.

Section: Regarding the statement that "the substance of speech is itself the indicative," the subsequent explanation holds that even common speech may directly receive this name. Speech that carries those names and so forth is capable of being indicative;
by subsuming the provisional back into the real, it reveals the substance through its function. Therefore, this is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

It takes the names and so forth as the direct designators (*vācaka*) and the designated (*vācya*). The meaning of "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*) is mental; names and other functions apply only in relation to the designated. Apart from this, there is no separate activity.
Because it functions [only] in relation to sound, its specific activity is said to reside solely in sound and not in names (*nāman*) and so forth.

Since there is no meaning of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) in relation to names and so forth, the *Yideng* (The Lamp of Meaning) states: "Names and so forth express that which they depend upon; they cannot be called 'informative' (*vijñapti*) speech."
All these [definitions] of "proximate" (*sāmantaka*) differ in their two meanings: being "concordant with the intention" (*anuloma-citta*) and "arousing the intention" (*citta-samutthāpaka*).

Since both are treated as "proximate," the term "intention" (*citta*) also indicates that it is a designation (*prajñapti*) identical to karma, consisting of body and speech; thus, they are analyzed using the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound, and for this reason, nothing further is said. Question: [Why is this so?]
To whom does this manifest [vijñapti] belong? Answer: It manifests only for oneself, because it is known by one’s own mind. Question:

Since the king and his subjects do not mutually perceive one another at the same time, how can they know [the action] such that the meaning of this manifestation is established? Answer: Because the former manifests the latter, and the latter knows the former;

thus, while they appear simultaneous in terms of moments (kṣaṇa), in actual principle they are sequential. Question: How is this different from non-manifest [avijñapti], since others do not know it? Answer: Non-manifest [action] is for oneself...
Furthermore, because it cannot be known. Question: What is the case with the Tathāgata? Answer: It is conceivable.

Regarding the passage "precepts are themselves liberation," this belongs to the category of *śeṣanirukti* (explanatory gloss), not *nirukti* (etymological derivation), nor is it *nairuktika* (lexical interpretation).

Section. Regarding the old term "precepts shared with concentration" (*samādhisaṃvara*): "shared" (*gong*) means "together" (*jù*). "Path" (*dao*) refers to the untainted (*anāsrava*); the meaning of "shared" is the same here.
"Dhyāna" (*chan*) refers to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); this is a distinction between the Chinese and Sanskrit terms.
Chapter. Regarding those who have previously explained terms such as "releasing" (*śīla*) and so forth: the ancient meaning is that good and evil follow their respective applications.
A single stream or category is termed "vinaya" (discipline). Furthermore, according to good and evil, there are respective protocols termed "vidhi" (rituals).
For example, the upāsaka constitutes one category; his rituals include the three daily observances and so forth. As for the non-discipline (*aśīla*), there is the distinct case of the tavern-keeper.
They constitute one category. In this manner, even down to the matters of setting up seats, seasonal adjustments, and sales, there are established ritual protocols (*vidhi*).
To say "no" to these is termed "unskillful" (*akuśala*); that which is not non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is termed "restraint" (*saṃvara*).

Section. Now, regarding the explanation that only those [precepts] which are virtuous receive the name [of "proper conduct"], it is said that what constitutes a model for emulation does not apply to the unwholesome.

This is because even if the unwholesome were to establish a pattern, it would be unworthy of being accepted as a model. It is like how one who is afflicted by defilements is called "lazy," even if they are diligent.
Chapter: On the Prātimokṣa as the Restraint (*saṃvara*). Question: Is it not the case that the name "restraint" refers to its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and function (*vṛtti*)?

How then can this non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) be understood as a *dharmadhāra* (possessing its own activity)? Answer: It is established based on the primary [informative action]. Non-informative matter follows the name. Alternatively, one first possesses the object (*dharma*) and then performs the activity of holding it;
such instances are numerous across the higher and lower [Abhidharma systems]. Furthermore, in the lower [system], there is yet another instance where the name "non-informative matter" is applied.
Section. Regarding the phrase "the nature is free from clamor and so forth": high and low are both [forms of] non-quiescence; being free from them constitutes quiescence. Section.

Regarding the phrase "the discipline is volition (*cetanā*) and so forth": because this concentration (*samādhi*) and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) depend upon present volition, it is explained as a *sāmīpya-ṣaṣṭhī* (proximate genitive).

The particle "zhi" (之) is a connective term. Alternatively, even in a proximate construction, a separator may be placed; or the meaning may be inclusive, following the *svasvāmi-sambandha* (owner-and-owned) analysis. Question:

Although this [unmanifest form] is established as "unmanifest" based on present volition, how is it included within the category of form (*rūpa*) under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)? Answer:

It is explained as being "proximate" by deriving the name from its function rather than its substance. Now, another interpretation states: "Proximate" refers not only to the mind or what is produced by the mind;
both are designated by their association with that [mind]. It is neither a possession nor a support; thus, both names appear together as being proximate.

Explanation: It may also be understood as taking the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) directly. This unmanifest is not established based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), nor is it called by the name of that concentration;
therefore, it is "proximate" (*sāmantaka*). Because it is superior and follows from that [concentration], it is explained as "proximate."

Section: Regarding "the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*). In the phrase "that which is beloved by those such as Jixuan [Jizang] and others," "beloved" is the general term that applies universally to all untainted (*anāsrava*) states, while "precepts" is the specific term.

Alternatively, "precepts" may be the general term and "beloved" the specific term; thus, it is analyzed as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. Now, this interpretation holds that "what is beloved" applies both to the cause and the fruit.

If "what is beloved" refers to the cause, then "what is beloved" is itself the precepts: the "precepts beloved by the Noble Ones. If "what is beloved" refers to the fruit, [it is the state of being beloved].
"Beloved by the Noble Ones" (*āryakānta*) and "the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*) are both explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound.

Regarding the phrase "those who lack restraint" (*asaṃvṛta*), one might ask: if "non-opposition" (*avirodha*) is itself the cause (*hetu*), it would be a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound; why then is it not so here?
The answer is: this prefix "a-" (*na*) is applied in relation to "restraint" (*saṃvara*), just as in the case of "ignorance" (*avidyā*), where it functions as a negation of action (*abhāva*).
Sixfold Exposition. Regarding the "non-contradictory cause" (*avirodha-hetu*), it is that which acts in contradiction when compared with what is not [the same].

Now, if this were to follow the non-contradictory cause, it could also be considered an act not conforming to the ritual (*akalpa*). If that [case] were to follow this [present case], one could likewise say that the sixfold exposition does not apply.

Section. Regarding the phrase "such as evil *śīla* (*duḥ-śīla*)": "evil" (*duḥ*) has the sense of obstructing defilement. It is called "evil *śīla*" because it shares the name "*śīla*" with [virtuous] *śīla*, yet is evil.
Here, this serves as an example to show that the various ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala-karma-patha*) are not termed "restraint" (*saṃvara*).

Just as these cannot be termed *śīla*, this is not an example cited by means of the six types of grammatical analysis (*ṣaṭ-vigraha*), because the character "evil" (*duḥ*) and the meaning of "non-" (*na*) are not the same. How so?
This is not explained by means of the sixfold method of analysis (*ṣaḍvidha-vigraha*). Question: If there has never been a person who possessed the precepts, upon what could this name be based?

And for one who has never possessed the precepts, in what would they be "evil"? Answer: When we speak of their "inherently evil nature" (*prakṛti-pāpa*), it does not necessarily mean that they must possess something [external] in order to be evil.
There may be those who hate others who are endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*); therefore, the Buddha cautioned against associating with them.

[Section] Regarding the phrase "The ancients explained... and so forth: The ancient interpretation holds that *śīla* is itself the precept (*śīla*). It is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*) and "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*), yet it is also called a precept;

thus it is named *śīla*. [Section] Regarding the phrase "From this difficult objection... and so forth: Since it is precisely evil, it does not prevent wrongdoing. Based on this, such an unwholesome dharma...

Regarding the title "Chapter on the Name of Precepts," as for the phrase "The present commentary says... and so forth: this is an objection concerning *śīla*. If one objects to "precepts" (*jie*), it should be understood by analogy with this.

Alternatively, the names and meanings of "precepts" (*jie*) and *śīla* differ: *śīla* means "cooling" (*śītala*) and is certainly not defiled or evil; whereas if "precepts" function to prevent what is non-virtuous...

The meaning is the same. However, if one says that the meaning of "preventing arousal" is broad—since it applies equally to preventing evil and arousing good, as well as preventing good and arousing evil—then when this meaning is applied to the previous objection, it shows a misunderstanding of the term.
Who would claim that I understand "precepts" (*śīla*) solely in the sense of preventing what is non-virtuous?

Rather, I understand "precepts" in the sense of preventing both [evil] arousal and [good] arousal. This is because the names "prevention" (*vāraṇa*) and "arousal" (*samutthāna*) are identical in their nature as formative activities (*abhisamskāra*). Based on this...

The difficulty now lies only in [interpreting] *śīla*. This reasoning may hold; however, the previous interpretation is superior, because whether one possesses the precepts or lacks them, as well as the receiving and relinquishing of the precepts, are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
Question: If one wrongly receives the precepts of a chicken or a dog, since these do not prevent wrongdoing, why are they called "precepts" (*śīla*)?
Answer: Because those [practitioners] adhere to them as a means of preventing what is unrighteous, the name and its meaning are likewise the same; it is only that they are falsely distinguished.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "neither restraint (*saṃvara*) nor non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)," the two instances of the character "not" (*fei*) are both interpreted as *na-vigraha* (negative determinative compounds) when viewed in relation to "restraint" and "non-restraint.

If it is "neither restraint," it is interpreted as a *viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* (descriptive compound) in relation to "non-non-restraint. This refers to that which is not non-restraint; namely, that which is wholesome, whereas the unwholesome is [non-restraint].

It is not non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) are different. This is explained by means of a *vyadhikaraṇa* (non-co-locative) analysis. Within this section, that analysis is reflected.
Since it has already been shown previously that the essential natures of giving (*dāna*) and striking (*prahāra*) are different, they are here summarized by implication.

If this were not an implied *vyadhikaraṇa* analysis, the word "also" (*api*) would have been placed as follows. If one says that within this context the two names are viewed in relation to one another, since—
If you argue that it is merely a "double negation" because the words of double negation do not denote anything, and thus one should not provide an explanation, this is also incorrect.
Why? Because even if the meanings were contradictory as being a single entity, an explanation could still be made.

Furthermore, if this is not a statement concerning a single entity, yet it is merely a double negation without anything denoted, then although these two negations cannot be separated from one another, they are like [the concept of] non-existence.
If one were to separate emptiness from existence, it would result in an error; therefore, no further explanation is provided. This interpretation accords with the text.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," this is explained by riding upon the preceding point that a single entity can simultaneously acquire two names.

Since both are "neither" [existent nor non-existent], they do not fall under the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍvidha-samāsa*); because this would not exhaust the full meaning, this further explanation is offered. Accordingly, whether wholesome or unwholesome, all may acquire these two names. Because...
Because this name is established within the context of *paryudāsa* (exclusionary negation), it is like how generosity (*dāna*) and so forth are neither vows (*saṃvara*) nor non-vows (*asaṃvara*).

Following this principle, the term is explained as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). However, by logical inference, it may also be explained as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) based on their mutual opposition;

yet, it does not entirely coincide with the "neither empty nor existent. Nevertheless, one should take the literal reading as correct, for the name is designated as being "intermediate" (*madhyama*), and thus it should be called "maintaining" (*dhāraṇī*).
Regarding the statement, "Karma may be so;
the restraint is the seed, etc.": the unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) receives its name based on the conformity between the supported and the support.

This citation of the support indicates that the essence of restraint is precisely the prevention of wrongdoing; it does not consist of the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates bodily or vocal action through preparatory effort. Therefore...

This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). Regarding the subsequent *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound): the volitions (*cetanā*) that manifest as the preceding and succeeding [moments] are termed "restraint" (*saṃvara*).

Since its essence is not non-informative (*avijñapti*), it is explained as a *tatpuruṣa*. This twofold explanation cannot be applied to the meditative (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*) restraints, because they are established based upon the volitions that manifest in accordance with the mind;
they are simply identical to the *svāgata* (welcoming) type. As for the *karmadhāraya*, it is not so called. Question: What constitutes the essence of restraint?

The basis (*āśraya*) is manifest thought (*vijñapti-citta*), and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) is its function, which is a derivative form (*upādāya-rūpa*). Why is it not permissible to explain this using the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound?
Answer: This is indeed possible. Even regarding that which depends on seeds (*bīja*), this same explanation may apply.

In the text, for the time being, since there is no distinction in their essential nature (*svabhāva*), the function is subsumed into the essence, and the essence is treated in accordance with the function. This is not explained by establishing them as distinct entities according to the system of the hundred dharmas (*dharmas*); therefore, they are not mutually exclusive.

This is incorrect. In the section below on "defining the essence" (*svabhāva*), it is analyzed in detail. Alternatively, in the preceding passage, terms such as "and so forth" (*ādi*) merely refer to the basis;

thus, "provisional non-informative matter" (*prajñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*) is formed using the *karmadhāraya* (attributive) compound. Nevertheless, the term "type" (*prakāra*) is used to express the general while implying the specific. By employing a general term, it reveals that this refers to restraint (*saṃvara*).

Since it is established upon the seeds (*bīja*), it also receives that name. This is explained using the *karmadhāraya* compound. If one follows this interpretation, then even though [restraint] exists in the meditative (*dhyāna*) and supramundane (*mārga*) states...

Two interpretations may be made. However, it is not "not so" (na tathā) because it does not rely on the name of the genus (*jāti*). Furthermore, it is also "not so" because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) as a dependent designation (*tatpuruṣa*) is distinct.

This refers to the volition (*cetanā*) currently manifesting before and after; whereas that which is the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or the path (*mārga*) is the essence (*svabhāva*) and its function (*vṛtti*).

Alternatively, according to the former interpretation, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) and the manifest volition are both included and collectively termed "maintaining one part of the restraint" (*saṃvara-ekadeśa-dhara*).

Regarding "karma" (action): it is also termed *dharmadhāraya* (possessive compound) when the action itself is held [as the object]. This is stated to distinguish it from the subsequent interpretation which holds that it is merely a *dharmadhāraya*.

It does not say "dependent compound" (*tatpuruṣa*), because by citing the general category, it is already implied that both are dependent compounds. As for the word "all," it refers to everything including non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and so forth.

If one follows this meaning, although the explanations of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*) also have two types, they lack the principle of being universally applicable to seeds; therefore, they are not [included here].
Thus it is. Among the "possessing the action" (*karmasādṛśya*), there are only the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*). Question:

Since the unmanifest of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*) is established based on present volition (*cetanā*), and is itself a manifestation, why is it called "unmanifest"? Answer: The unmanifest of the Prātimokṣa is not even known by oneself.

The unmanifest of meditative concentration and the Path is established merely on the basis of its being unknown to others; or rather, because its increasing function is not perceived even by oneself, with the exception that only a Buddha knows it thus. This is acceptable.

Regarding the statement that "volition (*cetanā*) has manifest form (*vijñapti-rūpa*) as its essence," some say that, following the analogy of a lamp, it also takes shape (*saṃsthāna*) as its essence.

Regarding the statement that "mental action (*manas-karman*) takes the former [manifest action] as its object," this is merely in accordance with the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*); one must apply such a correlation by reflecting upon the actions of body and speech. This is the principle.
It is indeed mental karma that also initiates [action], as has already been explained in the preceding chapter.

Regarding the section on intermediate karma, this distinguishes manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*). Herein, the initial explanation concerns those who are incomplete [in their faculties], because these possess only out-flowing (*sāsrava*) karma.

Section. Furthermore, regarding the "other wholesome qualities" of the Buddha, the *śīla* that gathers wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) which benefits sentient beings is termed "intermediate.
Question: Below, in the text of the section, the compiled meaning also permits that the *śīla* gathering wholesome dharmas be termed "intermediate.

Why is this [present position] refuted as being incorrect? Answer: While the *śīla* of gathering wholesome dharmas may be considered intermediate, here it is [the state] coextensive with the stage of Buddhahood; therefore, it is deemed incorrect.
Why is this? Because there are those who, due to the *kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering wholesome dharmas), are not yet fully endowed [with it];

such individuals who have not yet attained the proper mode of conduct (*dharma-naya*) are said to be "intermediate. This is not the case for the state of a Buddha, for all wholesome dharmas are fully accomplished therein, and that which is properly the mode of conduct is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*).

Therefore, the former interpretation is correct. Question: Although it may be so for a Buddha, why is the untainted (*anāsrava*) [state] not admitted during the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*)? It is said that only...

[Question: Is it the case that they take the *sāsrava* (with-outflows) as the primary [object]? [Answer: Within the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), even the *anāsrava* (without-outflows) are likewise complete according to their respective requirements.

One may practice all [virtues] equally within a single practice; this can also serve as a dharma-protocol. However, because it does not pertain to the intermediate state, it does not extend to the *anāsrava*.

In the subsequent text, the inclusion of wholesome qualities relies directly upon the *sāsrava*, and thus it does not state that "all" are included. [Question: When those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) turn their minds [toward Mahāyāna], do they perceive the preceding *anāsrava*?

Since it is not established [that they are both], why would everything not be included within the "neither" category? If that were so, then the first interpretation would again not be correct. Answer:

Because the informative expression (*vijñapti*) of that feeling is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*). This is discussed in terms of the essence of the feeling itself and does not concern its karmic activity; therefore, it is exclusively contaminated. Question:
Why is it said only that the Buddha’s body is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), worthy of emulation, and a standard for practice, and not others? Answer: For now...

Regarding the example of universal consensus (*prasiddha*) within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), since the state of being untainted (*anāsrava*) necessarily entails ethical discipline (*saṃvara*), one must reflect upon the fact that,
among the explanations for the arising of the stages in the sixth section below, only the latter interpretation is adopted.
Section. Regarding the statement that "the Buddha is equal [to others]": it is not only at the stage of Buddhahood that uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states arise;

they also arise as uncontaminated throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because they give rise to the two types of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*) of body and speech. Although the manifest karma thus produced is contaminated, the volition (*cetanā*) that produces it is pervasive across both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.
Section. Regarding the phrase "its distinct prātimokṣa, etc.": Above this, the manifest [action] (vijñapti) is explained; below, the non-manifest (avijñapti) is explained.

Although the intermediate non-manifest action is divided into two natures, it is likewise not specifically assigned to either non-discipline (asaṃvara) or non-non-discipline (na-asaṃvara); therefore, there is no contradiction.
Section. Regarding the phrase "by means of vows, one restrains volition" (*cetanā*) and so forth: the aforementioned three categories are all subsumed within this text;
therefore, those who occupy a middle position cannot be discussed separately, as they do not constitute a superior vow of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Section. Regarding the phrase "The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says, etc.": the various passages cited below all establish [the nature of] provisional designation (*prajñapti*).

This term "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to the vow for the formulation of the precepts, not the vow for enlightenment (*bodhicitta-praṇidhāna*). This is because the vow for enlightenment is initially cited as encompassing all bodhisattva practices.

Regarding this, the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Vijñapti* itself explains it as follows: "By means of the vow, the characteristics of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) are manifested and established," and so forth, up to "according to whether one performs good or evil."
Because there is a temporal limit, to what extent is that bodhicitta vow restricted?

Therefore, within this context, even regarding those who abide in non-restraint or the intermediate state, the *Śūyao* (Essential Pivot) explains in detail how these are called "equal vows" (*samatā-praṇidhāna*).

Furthermore, since this is precisely the vow for the precepts of the form aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*), what are the characteristics of these equal vows? Thus, there are many who have not yet reached a clear understanding regarding this passage.
To claim that [the text] "證等願極" (zhèng děng yuàn jí) is erroneous is a gross mistake; it is to act as a teacher in vain and a total lack of reflection. You ought to correct this immediately.

Yet, you remain stubborn and shameless regarding your own shortcomings, attempting to provide a forced interpretation before the great assembly, asking: "The precept-treasury for all future ages is established to its full extent—how could there be no limit?
Why would it not be the same? These words are devoid of meaning and contradict the spirit of the text. There is only...

One seeks Buddhahood in order to deliver sentient beings; this is because such words do not exist [in that context], and furthermore, because the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) herein can also be unwholesome (*akuśala*).
Regarding the phrase "this refers to either... and so forth: according to the commentary on that text, this passage contains seven meanings.

That commentary presents five meanings first and two meanings subsequently, though the sequence is not complete in the text. Now, following the main treatise, I shall briefly set them out in order. First:
First is the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*), which clarifies that the provisional is based upon the real. Second is the meaning of "arising" (*samutthāna*), which takes up the primary arising;

this excludes the two preceding types of volition (*cetanā*) and the subsequent moment, as well as the intermediate volitions that do not produce bodily or vocal action. Because those [intermediate ones] are connected to bodily and vocal actions, they are excluded from being "non-arising.

Third is the meaning of "ultimate" (*paramārtha*), which excludes middling and inferior volitions; although these may perfume seeds, they do not produce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), nor do they increase it.

Therefore: (4) Body and speech [are required], to show the basis for the manifestation of matter and names; (5) virtue and non-virtue [are required], to exclude the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is not established therein;
(6) the seeds of volition (*cetanā*) [are required], to distinguish it from active volition, because liberation (*vimukti*) is not established based on active volition;

(7) growth [is required], to distinguish it from the state prior to the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) or after the forfeiture of the offense, as those preceding and succeeding stages do not constitute non-informative matter.
Therefore, this does not refer to the Buddha. Since the Buddha’s stage is already perfected, even though there is no further growth, it is called "unmanifest" (*avijñapti*).

Now, examining the logic of the text according to the standard method of exclusion, the phrase "seeds of volition" (*cetanā-bīja*) can be understood in two senses: first, "volition" excludes other mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*);
thus, eight meanings of exclusion are established, while the commentary briefly omits one meaning.

[Question: Although it is not form, color, and so forth, since it is not a real color (*rūpa*), it must be a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). [Question: What then is it that is not volition (*cetanā*)? [Answer:

Regarding the "seventeen stages" mentioned in the treatise: the eight fundamental dhyānas, the eight preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) together are called the seventeen.
In this way, all [terms] are established by ceasing desire and evil; the root of the precepts (*śīla*) is established by ceasing what is unwholesome.

This is because one fears falling into the miserable realms (*apāya*), and it is not for the sake of ceasing the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) that the precepts are established. Question: It is commonly said that *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) refers only to the four dhyānas.

Why, then, does this text speak of seventeen stages (*bhūmi*)? Answer: The name is narrow, but the substance is broad. The original name refers only to the establishment of the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*). Thus, regarding the name and the substance...

Both [terms] are broad; however, to say that the name "dhyāna-restraint" (dhyāna-saṃvara) is narrow is incorrect. According to this, some claim that the term "dhyāna" (靜慮) is pervasive, but this is not so. The *Chang* (Chapter/Text) states:
"Regarding 'the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) co-arising with the Path,' Master Zhou says: 'This explains why the dhyāna-concomitant [precepts] do not extend to the untainted;
it highlights the superiority of the path-concomitant [precepts], but does not state that the dhyāna-concomitant [precepts] extend to the untainted. Or, it follows..."
In the Hīnayāna, these may appear to be distinct; however, in reality, the precepts associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*) also extend to the untainted (*anāsrava*).

Because they share the same essence as the precepts associated with the Path (*mārga-saṃvara*), yet are distinguished in their specific meanings—being conjoined with concentration and being conjoined with wisdom—they are established as two types of precepts.
Section. Regarding the phrase "The Abhidharma [states]... and so forth: this passage from the *Abhidharma* has already been reconciled; now it is cited again for further clarification. Section.

Regarding the phrase "The ten stages exist according to their respective applications": the eight fundamental stages—the Uninterrupted (*anāgamya*) and the Intermediate (*dhyānāntara*)—do not possess the seven preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
This has already been explained previously. Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate" (*yathāyogam*): the number of those who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and so forth is not fixed.

As for the passage "those who have already performed the action" and so on: why is it that not all [of them] possess the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) in conjunction?
It may be that this statement refers specifically to those who possess these qualities exclusively; or, it may apply throughout the entire major section.
Section Two: Regarding the two types of karma and the three types of karma, Master Zhou says: "The body and speech constitute two, and together with the mind, they make three.
As for why it is necessary to distinguish them as two and three: it is because they are explained in relation to both the Hīnayāna and the Mahāyāna.
The *Jixuan* commentary states: "The manifest and the unmanifest are designated as 'two. Within each of these two types of karma, there are three kinds of karma; therefore, it is said thus."

Regarding the passage, "That which is truly matter (rūpa) and truly informative (vijñapti)," these two meanings are real; they are called "real" because each is real in its own right, and they do not possess a separate substantial entity.
Regarding the passage, "But that which is neither karma and so forth," this is a designation based on a single meaning.

Section. Regarding "body, speech, and so forth": the preceding section distinguished conventional action (*prajñapti-karman*); this section distinguishes substantial action (*dravya-karman*). One sense is substantial; two senses are conventional.

The three instances of the character "non-" (*na*) refer to these three senses. They are termed "conventional" because they derive their names from their characteristics; it does not mean they lack a nature (*asvabhāva*).
In the *Chapters* (Zhāng), regarding the phrase "among the unmanifest forms (*avijñapti-rūpa*)": one is real and one is provisional; the meaning may be understood by analogy.
In the *Chapters*, regarding "dharmas that do not manifest": these are the things being prevented. Since there may be something produced [by them], they are not mentioned [here].
As for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), it necessarily has something produced; otherwise, the seven courses of action (*karmapatha*) would not be established.
Section. Regarding the phrase "first, the meaning of division (*bhāga*) and so forth," Master Zhou said: "To explain each one individually is called 'division' (*bhāga*);
to explain many types collectively is called 'category' (*varga*). Thus, the two meanings are distinct. My current interpretation is that "division" (*bhāga*) is synonymous with "stage" (*avasthā*).

When distinguished according to stages, they are termed "limbs" (*aṅga*) or "divisions. Therefore, both the [limbs] and the training (*śikṣā*) are called "limbs. Alternatively, it is like the divisions of chapters (*parivarta*) or sections.

The titles of the chapters are established by dividing them according to the sections of the text to be studied; later, the method of "explanation" (*vyākhyā*) is considered superior. As for "categories" (*jāti*), they refer to types or classes;
specifically, the seven categories of "limbs" (*aṅga*) are termed "categories of limbs," as will be fully understood below.
Section. Regarding the bhikṣu vow: if one speaks of being a bhikṣu or one who is fully ordained (*upasaṃpanna*), this does not constitute the bodhisattva precepts.
Section. Regarding the single factor of receiving full ordination: at the time of this initial reception, it is called "one factor."
"Chapter" refers to the one who performs the formal declaration (*jñapti*) for the fourth *karmavācanā*.

In the procedure consisting of one *jñapti* and three *karmavācanās*, the formal declaration is counted as the fourth by mentioning the two extremes while omitting the middle; thus it is called the "second *karma*" up to the "fourth.
The stage of requesting the precepts prior to performing the formal declaration constitutes the preliminary preparation (*upāya*) and is not included in this section.
Regarding the phrase "the chapters and the brief summary of the essential points" (*saṃgraha*), "coarse" (*audārika*) means "great," referring specifically to the heavy precepts.

Following the *karmavācanā*, one briefly indicates the characteristics of the four *pārājika* grave offenses so that the candidate may take them up. The above all concern the candidate as a constituent factor;
it does not refer to the recipient [of the transmission]. Question: According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the four *pārājikas* are first briefly explained.

Regarding the characteristics of upholding and violating [the precepts]: one may only confer the transmission after causing the candidate to give rise to a sense of affection and joy. Why, then, is it now said that the method is taught only after the transmission has already been conferred?
Furthermore, why is there no prior formal announcement (*jñāpti*) in that case? Answer: That refers to the Bodhisattva, while this refers to the Śrāvaka; therefore, they are not the same. Commentary:

When a Bodhisattva first encounters a teacher, it is necessary to first explain and demonstrate [the teachings] to cause them to take delight in them. For the Śrāvaka, however, he acts for himself first.
Since [the recipient] has already been examined when he was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), there is no need to first speak to him to inspire his devotion.
Once the ordination has been conferred, why would one not explain the precepts regarding what is to be observed and what is to be transgressed?

Furthermore, when a Śrāvaka receives the precepts by begging from the assembly, if the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) were recited without first making a formal announcement, the assembly would not be in harmony and their attention would not be focused. The Bodhisattva is not like this. Only...
Receiving from a teacher. To whom does one declare this?

[The] assembly [of scholars]. As for the *śrāmaṇera* and *śikṣamāṇā*, the original texts have not yet been seen; logically, one must reflect upon and rely on them.

Section. Regarding the phrase, "Although [the seeds] are produced by karma in the preceding stage," the following two lines are concessive arguments (*yukti*).

One should ask directly: "At the time when the seeds were previously perfumed, why were they not yet attained? After the ritual for the Dharma was completed, since one may even be without mind, why do they still increase?
These two initial sentences are the concessions; although at the time of requesting the precepts in the preceding stage...
The phrase "perfuming the basis so as to resemble the attainment [of the precepts]" refers to the two subsequent stages that bypass the preliminary vow.

The following sentence—"the intention being that because he was not yet full [of years], he had not yet attained growth, nor had he attained the *avijñapti* (unmanifest action), but now that the *karmavācanā* is concluded and his vow is fulfilled, only then does he attain the precepts"—explains this.

As for the statement, "At the time when the ritual is finished, although there is no mind [directed toward it]," etc., this concedes the point regarding the subsequent stage following the *karmavācanā*.
It continues to increase moment by moment until it is relinquished; even if one is without intention or possesses a mind of the three natures that is not conducive to growth, it still increases.

Furthermore, regarding the prior commitment, it is said that once the initial vow is fulfilled and the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is performed—from the first thought after the motion (*jñapti*) until the *karmavācanā* is concluded—the precept is acquired.
From the initial attainment of the precept until it is relinquished, it continues to grow without losing its momentum.

Therefore, this applies to both types of precepts, as both state that they exist even when one is without mind (*acittaka*). This merely clarifies their continued growth; it does not mean they persist solely from the moment of initial attainment until they are relinquished.

Consequently, the Bodhisattva precepts also apply to those who are without mind. When discussing the initial attainment and the time of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), there is a distinction between the Bodhisattva precepts and the Śrāvaka precepts regarding the presence or absence of mind;
thus, there is no contradiction. Based on this text, some say that the Bodhisattva precepts apply to those who are without mind.

It is obtained. That is to say, at the time of the *karmavācanā*, it is permitted that one who is without mind [obtains it]. This text states "the first moment and thereafter," not merely the first moment; what proof is there for that?

furthermore, the Hīnayāna has no basis for speaking of the three clusters of precepts (tri-skandha-śīla), which is precisely what is being opposed and refuted here.
There are many who fail to understand this point.

Section. Regarding the phrase "when this dharma-affair is concluded," etc.: once the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is finished and until it is relinquished, [the seeds] increase manifold in every moment.

because it increases manifold with every moment of thought, it is "not yet attained"; since the morality of a subsequent moment does not exist previously, it is not increased by the Buddha.
