Section. Now, as for the objection raised by those such as you: it takes the case of restraint (*saṃvara*) as an analogy for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), because [the latter] cannot be designated as such prior to its acquisition.
Section. Since this is so regarding restraint and the like, the later master provides an explanation by first restating the counter-argument: "Restraint also exists beforehand."

Because of the presence of forbearance and delight, why not say that one has already attained non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)? There are those who possess forbearance and delight but have not yet attained non-informative matter;
if we do not designate them as "restraint" (*saṃvara*) based on their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), what fault is there in this? Therefore, it is said: "It will be like an axe."
Section. Regarding the phrase "The later master’s explanation says... and so forth: since this has already been addressed as a substantive refutation, one should not resort to further reprimand;

rather, it simply returns to the previously established lack of a formal thesis. Question: The preceding objections and difficulties have ultimately not been avoided. How can both schools be free from such objections and difficulties?

Answer: The former master explains that unwholesome discipline (*duḥśīla*) is easily established and its non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is acquired first, whereas wholesome discipline (*suśīla*) is difficult to accomplish and is only established once the task is completed;
thus, they differ. The latter master explains that unwholesome discipline is easy to transgress, yet it is only when it becomes certain that it is formally designated as such.

Wholesome discipline is difficult to maintain, yet even if it might not be established, it is only at the moment of its establishment that it is posited; therefore, there is also a difference. Question: Is this so?
Regarding which master’s interpretation of the meaning is correct: the answer is that, according to the intent of the *Shuyao*, the former master’s view is correct.

There is another explanation stating that, according to the *Zuan*, the latter master’s view is correct, because it is said that the initial generation of the mind is still considered light, whereas when it has been practiced for a long time, it is termed "heavy."
[Section] Regarding the phrase "after the disposition has been made," etc.: this refers to cases where one dispatches a messenger to commit acts such as killing;

the offense is incurred only when the act is completed. Question: When one dispatches someone to kill a sheep, how does it apply to killing a pig? What if one orders that food be given to the Sangha, or that other things be given? Answer:

If there is no designated time or expectation, there is no fundamental karma (*maula-karman*). One should understand this by analogy; this is the reason why the offense of misappropriation (*miśra-prayoga*) is established. It must not be... [text ends].

There is no prohibition. The chapter states that there are those who receive [the precepts] spontaneously. This is the same as the "spontaneous" [attainment] among the ten types of attainment mentioned in the *Xuanjie* (Mysterious Explanation).

This interpretation is erroneous. It is not said that such [spontaneous attainment] does not exist after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; how could this spontaneous reception be absent after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa? One must reflect upon this.

Do not err. This refers to "spontaneity" (*svayambhū*) in the sense of being without a teacher; whereas the previous [case] referred directly to the non-performance of ritual acts, this spontaneity refers to performing the ritual acts oneself.
In the *Yogācāra*, there is indeed the self-administered *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act).
Section. If it is permitted for one to receive [the precepts] oneself and so forth, all that follows below is the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi*. This is all based on the person of the Śrāvaka.
If a Mahāyāna practitioner has already generated the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), they are permitted to receive them themselves, as in the *Sūtra on the Examination of Karma* (*Karma-vibhaṅga-sūtra*).

Even when reaching the stage of the *śikṣamāṇā* (probationary nun), self-reception is permitted. If a Bodhisattva wishes to leave the household life, they do so by leaving the household life [themselves]. Śrāvakas...
It is not so; because one must distinguish between what is capable and what is incapable, it is necessary to rely upon a teacher.
Regarding the section on "by means of six causes": first, impairment of intention, which refers to those who lack a sincere mind; second, impairment of the basis.
1. Those whose bodies are afflicted by illness; 2. those whose male organs are impaired, meaning their organs have disappeared and so forth; 3.

those who have impaired the white dharmas, such as those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), those who defile nuns, or those who live as thieves within the community; 4. those who are subject to others, such as when kings, parents, or others do not grant permission; 5.
those who act for the sake of protecting others, namely, those who are transformation-beings (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*).

Section. Regarding the phrase "except for omissions and deficiencies" (*vyavakīrṇa*): the preceding portion is the selection of the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*), while the following portion is the text on the selection of the teacher (*ācārya*).
The word "only" (*kevalam*) serves to define the scope; it does not appear in the main treatise (*śāstra*) but has been added according to the meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*).
The treatise contains the word "moreover" (*ca*). *Ācārya* refers to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), and *upādhyāya* refers to the preceptor (*śāstrī*). Some people lack understanding of this.
The practice is also deficient. It is not merely that there is no one to uphold it;
the preceptor who performs the formal ritual must necessarily possess knowledge. Furthermore, he must be of the same class as the assembly and, moreover, pure.

Regarding the single phrase "the two masters dispute the dwelling in pure precepts," its application differs for the two masters—whether it refers to the superior or the subordinate. As for the former master, the assembly must be pure.
To speak hypothetically: the later masters claim that the teacher need not be pure. This is incorrect.

The character "knowing" (知) in the phrase "not knowing [the teacher is] impure" is a scribal error; it should be the character "harmony" (和). This is because one does not harmonize with the teacher, nor does one rely upon harmony with him;
rather, one harmonizes with the Saṃgha. The *Jixuanjie* states: "It is simply through the three roots of seeing, hearing, and suspicion that one is pure. It is not...
If one knows that the preceptor is impure, one nevertheless obtains the precepts, because one does not formally beg for them from him. The *Jixuanjie* (Collected Explanations of Profundity) states:

"To say that one merely seeks to receive [the precepts] from the upādhyāya but does not beg for the precepts from him is incorrect. What difference is there in meaning between 'seeking' and 'begging'?
Furthermore, to say that the *karmavācanā* constitutes the upādhyāya is also incorrect; it should be said that this is how one obtains the precepts."
"Upādhyāya" refers to one who does not speak; it is also not the "personal teacher" (ācārya).

Regarding the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedure), although the name of the upādhyāya is not explicitly mentioned therein: Question: According to that *karmavācanā*, the name of the upādhyāya is indeed mentioned;
why then do you say the name is not mentioned? The text of the *karmavācanā* states: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This person, [Name] (this is said three times)..."

The name of the person receiving the precepts: the following follows the *Jixuan*. There are those who interpret this as requiring the mention of the *upādhyāya*’s name; this is incorrect. [The candidate] requests to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
This person, so-and-so, now petitions the Saṃgha for the bestowal of the full ordination. So-and-so (at this point, the name of the *upādhyāya* is mentioned) serves as the *upādhyāya*.

So-and-so declares himself to be pure and free from all obstacles, having reached twenty years of age, and being fully equipped with the three robes and the alms bowl. The Saṃgha now confers upon so-and-so the full ordination.

"Such-and-such a person is the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). Which elders consent? If the Saṃgha grants the full ordination (*upasampadā*) to this person with such-and-such a person as preceptor, those who consent remain silent;
those who do not consent should speak. The Saṃgha has consented and has completed the granting of the full ordination to this person with such-and-such a person as preceptor.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld. According to this, it is correct.

This refers to the name of the *upādhyāya*. Why do you say it does not refer to him? Based on this, Jìxuán interpreted these words as meaning that the name of the *karmakāraka-upādhyāya* is not mentioned.
My current interpretation is not so; it is certain that these words mean the name of the *jñapticaturtha-karman-upādhyāya* (the preceptor from whom one receives the precepts) is not mentioned.

One should answer: "In the place where the request for ordination is made, the *upādhyāya* is not specified; one simply says 'the assembly of monks' (*saṃgha*), clearly indicating that one is making the formal request."

The reception [of the precepts] takes place within the community of monks (*saṃgha*). For this reason, the *upādhyāya* need not be pure. This is because the role of the *upādhyāya* is merely to provide instruction;
it is not from him that one requests and receives the precepts. Question: In the *karmavācanā*, why is it said that one "requests the precepts"? Answer:
It is because the *karmavācanā* recites the words of the prior request for the precepts.

"Chapter. Regarding 'having already conferred the precepts' (*yǐ yǔ jì zhě*): it refers to having previously ascertained [the candidate's fitness] and granted permission to bestow them, which is termed 'having already conferred the precepts.
Fearing that the assembly might not grant its consent, one gathers the assembly to confer them; therefore, it is unnecessary to designate a *upādhyāya*.

Although the *upādhyāya* from whom one currently receives instruction corresponds to this role in the present age, he is not employed for this purpose; rather, a separate individual is established to take his place. As...
This refers to one's preceptor (*upādhyāya*).

Regarding the passage "the various masters" (*zhū shī děng*), Jíxuán (Ji Xuán) assigns these three characters to the preceding clause and consequently claims that the characters are erroneous, suggesting they should instead be read as "must be indicated.
I, however, maintain that they belong to the following clause; it means that [the author] makes his judgment based upon the various masters.
Regarding the chapter on the Bodhisattva precepts: the three clusters and the ten wholesome actions may be understood by analogy with what preceded.

As for the passage in the chapter stating that those among the five groups of monastics who receive the Bodhisattva precepts "should respect the precepts" and so forth, this takes various scriptural passages and treats them as a single uniform category; it is not a statement that exhausts the full meaning of the principle.

Section. Regarding the answer that "shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are increased by two causes and conditions": shame and dread of blame are twofold. First is the internal experience of shamelessness. As the treatise states:
"There are two kinds of distancing from immoral conduct (*duḥśīlya*): the undertaking of the factors of restraint and their subsequent protection, namely shame and dread of blame.
When one commits an offense, whether in the presence of others or in private, one feels profound shame; in this way, one distances oneself from immoral conduct."

Only by receiving and observing the auxiliary branches can one be fully endowed [with the precepts]; therefore, they are received from another. If shame (*hrī*) is present before one, there will necessarily also be dread of blame (*apatrāpya*);
however, one who possesses dread of blame does not necessarily possess shame. For this reason, the dharma of shame is the most powerful. Question:

Since shame and dread of blame pervade all wholesome states, why is there this distinction? Answer: As explained in the *Yideng* (The Lamp of Meaning), let us rely on a single characteristic for now: that which causes self-reproach necessarily involves others.
"Shame for others, not for oneself. Because one feels shame before others. Chapter.
"If one protects and upholds [the precepts] equally, there is no difference in merit. The *Śāstra* says:

"If there is someone who protects and upholds [the precepts] as deeply as they do for themselves, one should know that the merit produced is equal and without distinction. Next, below this is the previous passage: "Furthermore, if one gives rise to the thought..."

Regarding the passage [beginning with] "of oneself and others' offenses" (*ātma-para-āpatti-ādi*): this is the concluding text expressing the Master of the Commentary’s (*ṭīkākāra*) supportive intent. To be reproached by another is called "another's offense" (*parāpatti*);

to abandon [reproaching] others and reproach oneself is called "one's own offense" (*svāpatti*). As for "offense," it refers to that which belongs to another; other people are not considered here. If...

It is received only by oneself; because one does not guard against the offenses of others, it is common to both self-reception and reception from another. To cultivate and maintain restraint for both oneself and others is the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Regarding the phrase "from which other person," etc., two points are raised within the context of receiving from another;

however, they are omitted here as they are easily understood. One should explain them accordingly: [the vow is received] from a teacher and no one else. A "teacher" refers to the *ācārya* (preceptor) and the *upādhyāya* (preceptor-instructor); they must be pure and not...
It is not pure. Ji Xuan’s claim that the subsequent sections on the bodhisattva stages and so forth constitute the answer is incorrect, because the categories of meaning differ.
Furthermore, the subsequent passages discuss the manifest and the unmanifest, and do not open up the purity of the teacher.

Section. Regarding the phrase "if one receives [the precepts] oneself," etc.: this refers to the case where there is no teacher to manifest [the rite] through physical gestures (*kāyavijñapti*), which is termed "intentional manifestation" (*manovijñapti*).
It does not mean that there is no verbal expression, for the *Yogācārabhūmi* itself contains the ritual texts (*karmavācanā*). As it says in Chapter Forty-one:

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*), if he does not encounter a person (*pudgala*) endowed with all the necessary qualities..."
One should personally receive the Bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) before an image of the Tathāgata. One should receive it in this manner:
baring one shoulder, with the right knee touching the ground, or squatting or kneeling, one should speak as follows:

"I pay homage to all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, of the ten directions, and to the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*). I now wish, within the worlds of the ten directions..."
In the presence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one vows to undertake all the training precepts of a bodhisattva and vows to undertake all the pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva—

namely, the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).

Such training precepts and such pure ethical discipline have been fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past and shall be fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future throughout the ten directions.
All bodhisattvas of the past are now fully established in these rules of training and these pure precepts.

All bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in them; all bodhisattvas of the future shall train in them; and all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions are now training in them.
The second and third times should be spoken in the same manner. Having spoken thus, one should rise and make a formal announcement and request.

The proofs and so forth are all as previously explained. Furthermore, according to the *Zuanshu* (Compendium of Commentaries), regarding this [case], it does not exclude those who possess mental intention (*cetanā*).

There is no further verbal expression; rather, it is manifested solely through the mind. Thus, that text states: "If one receives [the precepts] spontaneously, there is only mental manifest action (*manas-karmapatha*)."

This does not take body and speech as its means (*upāya*); rather, it receives and attains the sevenfold non-informative (*avijñapti*) factors of body and speech solely by taking the mind as its means.

Although they are called "body and speech," they do not inform or indicate [an external object]. Question: Is there then a non-informative that does not arise from informative action (*vijñapti*), since there is no [actual] body or speech?
Answer: There is an informative action accomplished by the mind; therefore, the preceding passage above does not exclude mental volition (*cetanā*). This is shown in the subsequent passage below.
As explained previously, regarding the passage:
"Even if there are bystanders," this text serves as a general rebuttal to an objection. Whether one utters words or merely thinks in the mind, there must necessarily be bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

If there are bystanders who see [the action], how could it be expressed by the mind alone? This is used to resolve the issue because [the action] is not directed toward those bystanders. It is not [the case that it is not expressed].
Because it is intended to make others aware [of one's intention], it is not called a "manifest" (*vijñapti*) mark;
however, there are cases where it is indeed manifest, for "intention" (*cetanā*) is designated as "manifest" in relation to those bystanders.
Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* which states, "There is not even one person by the side," this refers to the *Saṃgītiparyāya-śāstra*.

Since this treatise allows for the existence of manifest action (*vijñapti*), does it not contradict the [Abhidharma] *Śāstra* which asserts that there is only mental manifestation (*manovijñapti*)? The general meaning of this [passage in the *Saṃgīti*] is as follows:

I do not say that there is definitely someone by the side, nor that there is no one at all by the side. This is what the *Śāstra* relies upon; it is based on the fact that there are absolutely no people by the side, and thus not even one person is present. So it is said.

Regarding "unmanifest karma (*avijñapti-karman*) for those who receive [the precepts] for themselves," it means that there is only mental manifestation (*vijñapti*); this is not contradictory. Each phrase consists of four characters, and its meaning is very clear.
As for the passage "now, facing the assembly, etc.," regarding one who performs self-confession: although there is no teacher, they do so by facing the assembly. It is not...
There are certainly no [beings] in the formless realm;

therefore, there exists manifest karma (*vijñapti-karman*). Regarding the passage "distant preparatory stages and so forth," this explains that in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the supramundane paths (*mārga*), there is the sense of being dependent on others:

"distantly" because they depend on the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the instructions (*avavāda*); "nearby" because they depend on the proximity to seeing the Buddha who provides the teaching. As for the phrase "properly arising," it refers to that which is properly able to initiate [the action].

This refers to the preceding thought-moment. Question: Since this precept of the path of concentration (*samādhi-mārga-śīla*) is not produced through a formal ritual act (*karmavācanā*), why must one insist on explaining its meaning as being received from another?
Answer: Because all the Abhidharma treatises state that it is "induced by what is received" (*upātta*). Otherwise, how could it be included within the category of form (*rūpa*)?

Section. Regarding the phrase "therefore it can only be said that [it is equal]," the question is: what does this imply regarding non-existence? The answer is: at the moment of recollection, it is non-existent because it is free from conceptual discrimination;
in relation to what follows, it is existent because there is subsequent cognition.
Regarding the passage, "Not the same as the preceding stages," etc.: based on this, the relinquishing of the precepts merely means they do not increase.

This text is very clear. How can those who are deluded claim it is distinct from transgression? They claim that when the substance [of the precepts] is stripped away, it is entirely non-existent all at once, which is called "relinquishing.

Therefore, one should say: that which has already increased in its function cannot be made non-existent. As for the case of the expiration of the period, it is analogous to the transgressor of a grave offense; first—
All cases are like this. Question: What is the difference between such an offense and "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*)? Answer: Only those of middling or inferior grades may be increased again;

this differs from abandonment. Abandonment can never be increased again; it is permitted only to be received again. An offense, however, merely requires that it be increased once the confession is completed, as it is not to be received again.
This is not mentioned in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-manasikāra-lakṣaṇa*, nor does it include its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the passage "The two types of manifest action, bodily and vocal, are like [the case of] relinquishment," some say that from this point downward, within the section defining characteristics, the relinquishing of manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*) is defined.

*Jíxuán* (集玄) states that from this point downward it serves as the condition for relinquishment; however, this does not reach the previous judgment. This text is precisely identical to the *Shìshù* (識疏) and the *Yìdēng* (義燈).
It refers solely to the first moment of thought. This must pertain to the beginning of a single lifetime, because that first moment constitutes the actual inception [of the action].

Since everything from its commencement until its completion is derived from that first moment, it is only this single moment [that counts]; the second moment and those following are not the actual point of inception.

One must not grasp at them. If one understands this, one will certainly not speak of the principle of "correctly initiating" [the practice], because the first part of each of the three sections is identical in its subsequent development.
There is also a tradition which says: "At the point of the word 'begging' (yāc), and at the point of the word 'desire' (chanda)."
Such various [errors] all stem from failing to understand the principle of the correct origination [of the factors].

Furthermore, some say that because body and speech each prevent origination at their respective beginnings, they fail to see the textual passages concerning mutual manifestation (*vijñapti*), nor do they comprehend the intended meaning behind establishing the [twelve] links.

This is as previously explained. One should understand the *Arthaviniścayasūtranibandhana* (The Lamp of Meaning) regarding "simultaneous" and so forth; there is simultaneity or non-simultaneity with respect to the body and speech.

Whether simultaneous or non-simultaneous, both depend upon the initial moment. That which is simultaneous is easy to understand; as for that which is non-simultaneous, although the seeds infused are distinct, [they are nonetheless related].

The establishment of these precepts requires only one [category] for each, because they mutually prevent the arising [of transgression]. As in the case of the body, the body establishes the prevention of seven [types of misconduct];

the same applies to speech. As previously cited from the *Za* (Compendium), there might be those who claim that body and speech are established separately, with the body preceding speech and speech following it, both being established based on speech.
Therefore, this statement was made to make it known that subsequent speech is not established based on that [preceding category], but is established solely based on what precedes it.

The body stands in the sevenfold posture, and speech is preceded by this; because this constitutes a single lifetime, it cannot have separate beginnings. It must certainly be the initial undertaking, because volition (*cetanā*) has but one beginning;
for a single volition cannot have two beginnings. Furthermore, it cannot be said that there are two distinct movements that initiate it.

Since it is initiated by a single movement, there is only one initial moment. It must be stated that they mutually express [the meaning], for once the textual principle is clear, one cannot entertain a different interpretation.

Furthermore, this text explicitly states that the point at which body and speech are first initiated is called "informative discipline" (*vijñapti-śīla*). Non-informative discipline (*avijñapti-śīla*) is established based upon this.
Therefore, regarding all passages concerning prostrating at the feet and requesting a teacher, why would one not take these as the actual initiation of body and speech?

If one considers that to be the definitive deliberation, how could it be so crude? If [you argue] that this is merely the text for requesting the teacher and not the basis for perfuming (*vāsanā*), [we reply:
the thirteenth fascicle of the *Zhengzhi weiyu* (Direct Pointing to the Only Language) states, "It is like the utterance of words when requesting the teacher," and so forth.
How can you not allow it to be established in the context of requesting the teacher? Moreover, since the subsequent text is also a request, if...

If it is argued that one has already initiated a bodily action (*kāyakarman*) by first prostrating at the feet [of the teacher], and thus must have already stood [in the position of the act], this is not correct.

That [prostration] is not yet an informative intimation (*vijñapti*), because the mind is originally subtle; it is merely a human matter established as a prior ritual of salutation. Since the movement of the desire to informate is employed immediately [at the moment of intent], although the *Zuan* states:
"The body initiates the seven limbs [of prostration]; like going to the teacher's place, one must not remain on the road," [this refers to the preparatory stage]. It is perfumed (*vāsita*).
Because it is based upon the precepts, the phrase "and so forth" below includes those who are present. Acts such as prostration and reverence give rise to that which is based upon the precepts.
Furthermore, there are cases where one merely sees [the recipient] and immediately requests, yet the matter is large and urgent and is not granted;

this depends on the recipient's own disposition—how could it concern the formal rules of the Dharma? Moreover, once the preliminary human courtesies have been completed, if one does not state what is being requested, when else would one wait? If...

As for the question of why one must kneel and prostrate to request [the precepts] after having already requested them, this has been explained previously: it is like a repetition at the moment of bestowal.
One understands that there will be no regression, and thus, increasing one's humility and reverence, one hopes for the bestowal. This is exactly as explained before.

Section: Regarding the statement that bodily and vocal actions are not initiated by this [homogeneous cause] (*sabhāgahetu*), it has already been established previously that they do not arise from it.
As the *Arthaviniścaya-pradīpa* states: "Momentary origination" (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*) refers merely to the mutual induction of moments from one moment to the next.
Section. Regarding "existence, non-existence, and the three natures": because these natures differ from the preceding [discussion], they cannot be grasped [in that manner]. Question:

If the principle of the three natures being indeterminate is thus, how can there be this thought of existence or non-existence? Answer: This previous [statement] refers to the period after the second moment; it does not preclude the time when mind exists or does not exist thereafter.
Alternatively, the characters "existence" (you) and "non-existence" (wu) may be connected in meaning with the three natures; they simply refer to the three [natures] themselves.
Regarding the phrase "of indeterminate nature": this is stated generally, intending only those whose virtuous nature is indeterminate with respect to existence or non-existence.
Furthermore, "virtuous" here refers exclusively to virtuous precepts (*śīla*). As for the unwholesome, because it arises moment by moment, only its simultaneity is mentioned;
or perhaps it is also [present] from the beginning. The term "simultaneous" refers to not being twice [separate], nor does it mean "only. Moreover, it merely discusses...
First: Because [the state] may also be without mind and so forth even after that point, this follows the latter interpretation.

Regarding the passage "The Buddha is not like this," some say it refers to a careful examination of the statement regarding the relinquishment of the non-informative (*avijñapti*), while others say it refers to a careful examination of the statement regarding the relinquishment of the informative (*vijñapti*).

According to the character "然" (ran), the latter interpretation is superior. This is because one who has recently abandoned the informative is not yet called "one who has relinquished" [it], even though [they have indeed ceased it].

One does not abandon the *vijñapti* (informative action). However, it is also impossible to further produce the *avijñapti* (non-informative action). Alternatively, one may take these two together as the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*).
Yet, the character "然" (however/also) separately connects to the production of the *vijñapti*. Based on this meaning, it is said that "it is not so.

Although the seeds do not increase and the present [action] lasts but a moment, neither is termed "abandoned. Having thus established the point following the preceding inquiry, one might fear a doubt arising, asking: "Since..."

The Buddha possesses manifest action (*vijñapti*), which should give rise to non-manifest action (*avijñapti*); therefore, this [text] precludes it without needing to state the underlying principle, because it is already complete and no further perfuming occurs.
The character "condition" (*yuan*) at the end of the line "abandoning the lower" is now suspected of being redundant.

It appears that Master Jixian saw this character "condition" and judged everything following "its body" (*qishen*) to be "conditions for abandonment. This is not the case, as has already been explained above.

Section. Regarding what is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are likewise fifty-three [precepts]. Among the first four branches, the second branch is named "the locus of training" (*śikṣāpada*).
Now, this must apply to all loci of training; apart from the four root [offenses], all others are subsumed herein.

To resolve to abandon them with the thought, "I shall no longer train," is called "abandoning the precept. Since these are light offenses and do not constitute abandonment, one resolves [to continue training].

Only through renunciation is the precept abandoned. To resolve to abandon it also constitutes abandoning the root, because the characteristics are similar and because even an inferior [resolution] has this effect.

The training rules (*śikṣāpada*) within the three types of wrong precepts are to be understood accordingly; their formulation is broader. Pure precepts (*viśuddha-śīla*) are precisely the root precepts.

Alternatively, this vow of abandonment also extends to the root precepts, as one might abandon them out of apprehension of future transgressions even though one has never actually committed one. This is explained below.

Section. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and the Bodhisattva precepts, etc.": although the preceding [section] has reconciled the textual passages, it has not yet reconciled the correct interpretation of the similarities and differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Therefore, the word "furthermore" (又) is placed here to indicate an additional point. Moreover, since the preceding section reconciled the sūtras as being of expedient character (化相), and because it was still possible to interpret the bhikṣu [precepts] in the same manner as before—given that the sūtras describe them entirely as being of expedient character—it is for this reason that the preceding reconciliation of the sūtras is set aside;
setting the former apart, one further addresses the actual abandonment (實捨) as well.

This differs from the previous interpretation; therefore, the word "also" (又) is placed here. Some say that from this point downward, the three grades of bodhisattvas all relinquish [the precepts] and become identical to bhikṣus.

Thus, the subsequent text states: "Nor by a superior entanglement (*saṃyojana*). The *Jixuan* (集玄) changes the character "also" (亦) to "superior" (上), intending to bypass the textual phrasing to mean that while an offense committed through a superior entanglement results in loss [of the precepts], an offense not committed through a superior entanglement does not result in such loss. My current interpretation of these words is as follows: Bodhi...
The character *sa* (薩) is the same as before, but the term *bhikṣu* (苾蒭) differs; likewise, the characters are not erroneous.

However, one must inquire whether the usage of "also" (*yì*)—whether it is the superior [usage] or not—is subject to loss or non-loss; this is its general meaning. "Also" (*yì*) is explained as being the same as before.

By contrast, it reveals that for the *bhikṣu*, it need not be the same as before; rather, it is essential that all be relinquished. Using the text in this manner and examining the Sage’s intention is most exquisitely subtle.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The Nirvāṇa Sūtra says... and so forth, the detailed determination will be provided below. If one were to completely abandon [the teaching], it would not mean a lack of understanding;

therefore, each case admits of both abandonment and non-abandonment. To completely abandon and to completely deny [the teaching] are both instances of a lack of understanding. That master, however, instead interprets the meaning of this refutation as actually being an abandonment;
he does not realize that even the denial of the manifested aspect (nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa) is also called "understanding."

Section: Regarding the four reasons for relinquishment (*prahāṇa*): the first two are merely different in terms of being mental or verbal, yet both constitute a relinquishment through regression (*parihāṇi*) and are subsumed under the *bodhicitta*.

Although the latter two differ in being the root or the derivative offenses, they are both *pārājika* (defeats) and are likewise subsumed [under the *bodhicitta*]. This is based on the principle that there is no increase [in the gravity of the offense] compared to the preceding cases, and thus distinguishes between the root and the derivative.
The mention of "categories" (*prakāra*) within the derivatives follows the same logic as the root. This is the first interpretation; each point is identical to what was stated previously.
The second is the condition (*pratyaya*). That which is called "conforming" (*anuvartin*) has the meaning of being of the same class (*sabhāga*).

For example, it is said that all five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) possess corresponding offenses of the same class; thus, the offense of defiling one's mother is an offense of the same class as killing one's father or mother.
All such cases are detailed in the *Yogācārabhūmi*. This case here is likewise. These four types of offenses of the same class are termed "conformities" (*anuloma*). Question: As for...
What are their characteristics? Answer: For example, the act of slandering the Triple Gem through wrong view is designated as the root [offense].

Those who destroy it are of the same category. Furthermore, just as the destruction of another’s generosity through stinginess is of this same category, so too are the others, though they cannot be fully demonstrated here;

one should consult the texts again later. Moreover, the distinction between root and derivative [offenses] may be explained in terms of the person: the root is the primary act, while the derivative assists it.
These are the two distinctions of this chapter.
Regarding the phrase "the fundamental bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth," this is the second interpretation; it explains that the two aforementioned conditions are likewise distinct.
There is no restatement here of the difference between the root and the derivative [defilements], as the categories mentioned in the previous two conditions are identical to what is stated here.

This refers to the category [of offenses]. That is to say, regarding the Bodhisattva grounds, we shall first explain those that are concordant (*anuloma*). In this way, among the four original categories and three sub-categories, all are abandoned;

because the concordant is considered more serious, it is abandoned only when the superior grade of the concordant is reached. Subsequently, the lower grades are transformed accordingly. If one does not perform this abandonment according to the categories, it would not be the same.

Thus, between the original and the concordant, what is the distinction between light and heavy? How could their abandonment differ? In the *Jixuan* (Collection of Mysteries), the original and the concordant are treated as follows:

Regarding the "inherent prohibition" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*): this [interpretation] is far too broad. How could one abandon the precepts merely by committing a transgression? What is now being said—that even a slightly light offense may be so—is acceptable.
Although it is light, it is still subsumed under inherent prohibitions; yet it does not fall among the forty-eight minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*).
It is simply a case of a slight reduction within the category of heavy offenses. Is there anything that surpasses the *pārājika* offenses? Furthermore, regarding the forty-eight...

The previous statement that these are merely *pratideśanīya* (offenses requiring confession) is incorrect; it is erroneous and utterly thoughtless, failing to take the matter into proper consideration.
How could acts such as setting fires, engaging in sexual intercourse, taking life, or destroying the Three Jewels be mere *pratideśanīya* offenses?

One must exert effort to reconcile them; do not neglect this task. I shall not alter my question. Question: What is the distinction between these and the grave (*sthūlātyaya*) offenses? Answer: [As follows:]...
The fourfold meanings of the causal conditions and karmic actions pertaining to the ten grave offenses are precisely what distinguishes them from the light offenses.
Were it not so, why would they not be mentioned as such among the light offenses? Since they are not mentioned among the light offenses, those four do not fall within the category of the light.

The gravity of actions such as killing is determined by whether they possess four specific characteristics that lead to rebirth in the Avīci Hell; those lacking these characteristics lead instead to other hells.

Possessing these four characteristics constitutes non-restraint (*asaṃvara*); lacking them constitutes the intermediate state (*madhyama*). Thus, both categories of killing and so forth have varying degrees of lightness and gravity.
These twenty distinctions have been briefly explained; it would be difficult to detail all their remaining specific characteristics exhaustively.

[The author] states: As in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are both light and heavy [offenses] for praising oneself and disparaging others. My own commentary (*zhuàn*) explains: that which is not done for the sake of fame or profit is called a light offense;
this refers to cases where it is a superior point for another. Question: Under which of the four meanings is that which is done for the sake of fame or profit subsumed?

If it is not subsumed, there would be something left unaccounted for. Answer: It is subsumed under "livelihood" (*ājīva-karma*), or else within the category of "conditions" (*pratyaya*). Here, "condition" means "to act for the sake of. This...
The interpretation as "superior" is correct.

Regarding the passage "Furthermore, those who retreat from the bodhicitta," etc., it must first be that they have retreated and abandoned the bodhicitta; therefore, this interpretation is the correct one.

Regarding the question, "As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*," etc.: since what has been received is identical [in both cases], why is it not the same for abandonment? The general meaning of the following answer is as follows.

Although their outward appearances are the same, how could their minds not differ? For this reason, the conditions for their relinquishment are likewise not the same. Regarding the response in *Jíxuán*:
the character "棄" (discard) in the lower section has been changed to "受" (receive). My current interpretation is that since the first phrase is cited separately, there is no need for such a change.
Furthermore, what has been rejected by the [previous] eyes need not be altered. Jixuan also relied on the text of the subsequent chapter to change "pride" (màn) to "indolence" (màn).
My current interpretation is that when the movement of the mind is expansive and its duration through time and kalpas is long, not seeking a swift end is termed "pride" (màn).

As it is said in the world: "The great ocean does not concern itself with the fragrance of a ladle; rather, through many kalpas and many lifetimes, it must be perfumed. Is this not a sign of a broad and unhurried mind?
Furthermore, can one who is hasty be considered a vessel of greatness? It is like a pot that has been scorched and is about to crack open when one wishes to open it.
Question: The seven classes of followers are themselves the bodhisattva vows. Since their characteristics are subject to doubt, how can one receive them within a single body?

[They are] the seven assemblies (*saptasaṃgha*), because their rules of conduct (*ācāra*), branches, and physical characteristics are all different. If categorized by their constituent parts (*aṅga*), one should say that a bhikṣu possesses all seven assemblies.
Even if [one were to argue] otherwise, it is impossible; for if one were to receive them again later, it would contradict the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

If they were received as seven bodies (*kāya*), how could there be a single reception without a repeated reception? Furthermore, in the ritual text (*karmavācanā*) for receiving [the precepts], it says "one... [and so forth].

One must strictly observe the precepts. One receives them as a single body; how could one possibly receive them all? What is meant by "categories"? It refers to the distinct categories of each of the seven groups of practitioners. How are they distinct?
They certainly do not accord with the texts on *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures), because the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) for all [seven] groups are common to them.
Answer: It should be said that because the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) of a bodhisattva is extremely vast and extensive, it extends from this present life until the end of time.
Regarding the future body, its form is immeasurable; whatever kind of body it may be, one maintains this precept in all such forms. Therefore, one accepts it in this way.

One accepts the seven [precepts] within a single body because a bodhisattva does not feel shame for having a female body, knowing that it will certainly not remain solely of this one type, and because it is not fixed that one will not receive a female body.
Furthermore, one knows that if it is beneficial, one must accept it. Otherwise, it would not be exhaustive.

In future lives, one shall never again receive [the precepts] repeatedly. One must reflect and deliberate; do not err, do not mistake. Question: Regarding the ten inexhaustible precepts (*daśāvaśeṣa-śīla*), should they be fully received throughout all future bodies?
Answer: Those are precisely these; it does not matter what kind of body one possesses, for they are complete within the seven.
Otherwise, the mind and the words would be inconsistent, and it would not be due to delusion of mind. A single body alone cannot exhaust them.

[The following] chapters [discuss this]: Regarding those who do not receive the Bodhisattva precepts and so forth, Jíxuán and others state that if one receives the Bodhisattva vows with a distinct mind, they are both relinquished at two specific times.
This is because there is a separate reception [of the vows] when a Bodhisattva teaches and transforms sentient beings according to their various types, or when following a sage.

In instructing and transforming sentient beings, one must follow their individual capacities; the preceding interpretation serves as the foundation. There is a textual passage in the following chapter:

"If, in a future life, one abandons [the vow]," etc. Regarding this, the *Jixuan* commentary states: "The two characters 'sheng-fen' (birth-portion) are an error in transcription. According to that treatise, it says:
"If there is no abandonment of such a discipline, one should know that it continues to function in other lives as well. It is not [the case that it ceases].
Regarding "he abandons": the word "or" (vā) is not an error; this phrase is first cited [from the source]. One who has passed away is called "abandonment of the basis of birth" (*janma-bhāga-tyāga*);

this indicates that he does not abandon the bodhisattva precepts. This constitutes the section on the four conditions for abandoning [the precepts] from that treatise; first, the non-abandonment is analyzed, and subsequently follows the text concerning abandonment through the aforementioned four conditions.

Regarding the phrase "the precepts for leaving the household life and so forth": as for those who receive them in the "pavilion" (loutuo) manner, if they are like those who receive them all at once, their vow is that they shall be maintained until the end of future existences, such that even if their bodies are transmuted, they shall not be abandoned.
Alternatively, for those who directly resolve their minds [to observe them] throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, this applies to the exhaustion of the future;
it does not fall within the scope of the previous vow to maintain them only for the duration of one's physical life.

Regarding the phrase "immediately after saying 'many days,' etc.": this is further based on other sources. Since both the *upāsaka* (lay follower) and the *upavāsa* (one-day vow) involve a specific period of commitment, if there were no provision for exceeding that limit, it would indicate that receiving these vows separately is permitted in this manner;
yet, it must still be capable of withstanding textual scrutiny.

Section. Regarding "those who do not attain the distinct [attainment]": if one has not generated the mind through the aspiration and vow of a bodhisattva, one cannot enter the distinct [path] beyond the unestablished (*apratiṣṭhita*).

Section. Regarding "if a different category arises": this refers to differentiation. The three realms, the nine stages, and the distinct classes of the three periods of time are all termed "differentiated parts" (*bhinnabhāga*).

Section. Regarding the four conditions: the first one and the last two are entirely relinquished. As for the relinquishment of the portion of receiving the precepts, it is entirely indeterminate. Section.
Second, regarding the relinquishment of receiving the precepts: if one receives the precepts without having previously made a vow to relinquish them, even though [the precepts] exist...
Confession does not necessarily require a vow of renunciation; therefore, it is established as a separate condition.
The chapter states: "If one receives the precepts temporarily," this clarifies that they are not permanently relinquished.

Once the period of aspiration has been fulfilled and the virtuous discipline (*kuśala-śīla*) is subsequently abandoned, there is no need to commit evil, for it would instead constitute non-discipline (*aśīla*), according to the original intent. Thus, there are cases where [the precepts] are definitely relinquished, as cited later.

Because it is fixed. Regarding the statement "four karmas," the *Jíxuán* (Collection of Profound Mysteries) amends "four" to the character "thought" (*cetanā*). There is an interpretation that the three [karmas] of body and the one of speech constitute four;
or [they are categorized as] those to be experienced in the present life and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "The *Yogācārabhūmi* says... and so forth: this means that even when one temporarily suspends the precepts (*śīla*), they are still said to be "not yet relinquished" because they have not been permanently relinquished.

Regarding the passage beginning with "It does not say 'suspension of the precepts'...": it means that once the characteristics of the suspension of the precepts have been described and the vow has been fulfilled, from that point onward, it is termed the "permanent relinquishment of non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*).

Section. Regarding the phrase "the meaning is analogous to the vow and so forth": since it has been stated that the time of relinquishment has a fixed limit, it does not preclude the fact that for those who possess [the requisites], there may also be variations in duration.

Based on this, the relinquishment of the requisites is explained according to each specific branch as liberation; thus, there is indeed one person who bears both names: "one who possesses the discipline" and "one who does not possess the discipline.
Question: At what point is the vow exhausted, and by what condition is it relinquished? Answer: This belongs to the category of relinquishment.

It is subsumed within the first object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because aspiration is also subsumed therein. Since the cessation of evil aspirations necessarily gives rise to the relinquishing of aspirations, they are mutually exclusive by their very nature.
Alternatively, it is the second object-condition among those that enter into the middle state.

Section Three: Abandonment at the End of Life. Because the force [of the vow] has reached its limit, and because one abandons the force through the fulfillment of the vow. Question: Since the vow pertains to many lifetimes, is it not abandoned at the end of life?
Answer: The principle of sustaining life applies only to a single lifetime; therefore, those individuals do not realize that [the vow] extends across many lifetimes.

This is because one who knows [the consequences] does not persistently commit evil. Alternatively, it may be subsumed under "at the end of life," as one also dies and relinquishes [the precepts] during subsequent intervals.
This must be examined in detail. Section Four:

Relinquishing through Attaining Meditative Absorption (*samādhi*). Question: At the time of attaining meditative absorption, one must first possess the precepts (*śīla*). Why is this specific condition mentioned?

One does not receive the precepts because one lacks a human body. Answer: One cultivates the volition of collective retribution; it is not that the mind is constantly associated with the volition of the precepts.

However, as long as there is a remote reliance upon the precepts, it is still possible. This is like one who previously received the precepts, but when their period of commitment expired, they instead became one who possesses non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).

Thus, because the cultivation of concentration relies upon prior morality, one abandons subsequent non-discipline; therefore, this condition is necessary. Furthermore, even a partial morality can serve as a basis.
It is said that those who possess no morality at all, or even lack the Three Refuges, will certainly not obtain a human body.

In this classification, those who possess morality as appropriate have not abandoned it; however, because they abandon it through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), those who merely take the three refuges may attain a fortunate rebirth (*sugati*) yet do not abandon immorality (*avirati*).
Those who cultivate meditative concentration based on such morality, however, do abandon immorality.
It is taught that even those who lack ethical discipline (*asaṃvara*) may possess the capacity to induce meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the butcher Viśāla-lalāṭa demonstrated this very sign.

Regarding the statement by some that "the physical form perishes" and so forth, one should reconcile it with the *Yogācārabhūmi*, for since the four conditions are not exhausted therein, this [position] is not superior.
Section. Furthermore, as for the statement that this is not so: it is not the case that the evil precepts (*duḥśīla*) are difficult to relinquish.
Section. Regarding the concession that these two types are equal: even when the physical form (*liṅga*) disappears, the true principle is that one does not relinquish the precepts;
because the two sexual organs do not cause the relinquishment of the lay follower (*upāsaka*) precepts, it is stated in general terms that they are not relinquished in their entirety.

Section. Regarding the abandonment [of the precepts] due to six conditions: the first five conditions apply to both the wholesome and the unwholesome; the sixth type applies exclusively to the abandonment of the wholesome.

Alternatively, within those [six], it may be intended to illustrate the abandonment of the unwholesome through the reception of the precepts. If that is not the case, in what category is this condition included?
Section. First, "by the abandonment or destruction of the volition of undertaking" refers to the renunciation of one's vow. Second, "the completion of the designated period":

here, pure faith and afflictions are designated as wholesome and unwholesome respectively. Third, "the completion of the action": even if the designated period has not expired, the [unmanifest] is abandoned once the matter is finished;
this refers to the completion of one's own action. Fourth, "when what was given by oneself is entirely destroyed by another," the unmanifest is then abandoned.

Section. Regarding the phrase "if [it is] equal within the bodhisattva precepts": since this section has already analyzed the *śīla* of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla*), it is clear that this precept is practiced in the state of the middle way (*madhyama*).

Question: This would contradict what was stated previously, namely that the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) of the middle way is correctly defined as being with outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the *śīla* of gathering virtuous dharmas can also be without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Answer: It is not stated here that all [instances] are exclusively of the middle way; rather, it should be explained as follows.
Excluding the Buddha and the causes that are untainted (*anāsrava*), because those various *dharmas* are not deficient in their suitability, they are included within the restraint (*saṃvara*).

Now, we shall discuss the remaining minor forms of giving and so forth, which are the accumulation of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka*); however, as these are not the proper rules of conduct (*ācāra*), they fall into the category of the intermediate state.

For this reason, it is said that through small acts of giving and so forth, one enters the previous six causes to distinguish renunciation (*tyāga*); those [causes] such as the untainted are not applicable here.
Regarding the abandonment based on these six causes:
the section states that "excluding these constitutes abandonment," meaning that by excluding the condition of death, there are only five.
Alternatively, the section states that "adding six" is also possible, because there are limits reaching up to the end of life, or because it refers to the regression from bodhicitta.

The *Cittabhūmi* (Mind Section) states: "For now, it is said that [the category of] 'gathering wholesome qualities' (*kuśalasaṃgrāhaka*) exists, while the other two also exist. Now, one asks: where else could the restraint (*saṃvara*) exist?

It should be stated that wholesome restraint has already been included within the six causes mentioned in the preceding text. One should consider the benefit-bestowing precept (*anugrāhaka-śīla*) according to this principle.

There are two possible ways in which gathering wholesome qualities and benefiting others may be categorized: they may reside within the intermediate category (*madhyama*), or they may reside within the restraint. Question: Thus...

The three categories (triskandha) are also subject to mutual confusion. Answer: If one refers to the three categories as such, they are not termed "restraint" (saṃvara), because they are established separately.

Furthermore, within the context of restraint and non-restraint, there are distinct designations for that which constitutes restraint, such as the inclusion of wholesome factors (kuśalasaṃgrāhaka) and so forth.
Thus, the three categories and the three types of restraint are each definitively different. There is a difference in the breadth and narrowness of the restraint in these two locations. If...

If it were not so, how would one reconcile this with the previous statement that the *kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering virtuous qualities) at the stage of Buddhahood is included within the *vinaya-vinaya* (the code of discipline), because it serves as a model for practice?
Regarding the reference to the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī* in Chapter Seventy-Eight: that text itself enumerates the *sūtra*, the *vinaya*, and the *mātṛkā*.
In the *Sūtras*, there are four, nine, or twenty-nine matters; in the *Vinaya*, seven aspects are taught; and in the *Mātṛkā*, eleven aspects are taught.
Regarding the seven [aspects] of the *Vinaya*: first, the teaching on the procedures for undertaking training;
second, the teaching on matters conducive to the grounds of defeat (*pārājika*); third, the teaching on matters conducive to transgressions.

Regarding the "matter" (*vastu*): fourth, because it proclaims the nature of an offense; fifth, because it proclaims the nature of non-offense; sixth, because it proclaims the emergence from an offense;
seventh, because it proclaims the relinquishment of the vows. As for what is called "matter," it should be subsumed under the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*;
therefore, it is termed "the finger. However, even in the absence of these words, it may be designated as "the finger."

Section. Regarding the view that bodily action (*kāyakarman*) and so forth [are distinct]: verbal action is a designation based on vitarka and vicāra; this alone is explained as before. Since bodily action is not like that, it is therefore explained separately.

Because volition (*cetanā*) is the essential substance of action, it pervades all three [types of action]. This interpretation is correct, for it allows for the undertaking of precepts (*śīlasamādāna*), and because one does not create actions of a lower stage while in a higher stage.
Furthermore, the consciousness borrowed [by those in the formless realm] is merely neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Section. Regarding the phrase "as for those that are untainted (*anāsrava*)," above, in the discussion of the tainted (*sāsrava*), there were two masters; below, in the discussion of the untainted, there is no further distinct interpretation. Section.
Regarding the phrase "such as the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses," it is feared that an external objection might be raised: "The Buddhas always abide in the fourth dhyāna. Above...
In the absence of vitarka and vicāra, how could there be bodily or vocal [action], or how could there be speech? This question may be understood according to the two preceding masters.
The subsequent answer by way of example is as usual and may be understood accordingly.
[The] Chapter [states]: "How could those World-Honored Ones... This raises the fruit to reveal the cause; it is because the World-Honored Ones still exist as previously cited.
[The] Chapter [states]: "It is certainly untainted (*anāsrava*). It is certainly so. Because it does not say "only," there is no contradiction.

Since it was previously stated only that the untainted *prātimokṣa* exists in the eight stages, this statement is made to show that it extends through all ten stages for those of gradual enlightenment.

Prior to the stages (bhūmi), all [precepts] are universally unoutflowed (anāsrava). Receiving the prātimokṣa precepts is universally based upon the higher stages; it does not exclude the outflowed (sāsrava), nor is it necessary to fully relinquish them.
Regarding the *Lushenafo jing* (The Scripture of Buddha Vairocana): this is the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*; it is given that name because it was spoken by Vairocana. (18)
Regarding the Brahmā deities, the general consensus among the commentators is as follows: there are three heavens in each of the first three dhyānas, and nine in the fourth dhyāna;
excluding the Heaven of Non-conception (asaṃjñisattva), Mahāśvara is included. Consequently, a question was raised: "How can those in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens receive the precepts?

Since they possess a fixed nature, they lack the arousal of the resolve [for awakening]. To this, he replied: "The words are general, but the meaning is specific," or alternatively, "They are not ignorant of the Dharma," and thus their reception is permitted.

All [the sūtras] uphold this; or, it may be based on the perspective of manifested forms (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Now, I say it is not so. As in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, apart from the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens, there are eighteen others.

Above the first three dhyānas, one is added to each, which constitutes their collective name: the Brahmā Heaven of the First Dhyāna, the Ābhāsvara Heaven of the Second Dhyāna, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven of the Third Dhyāna.
There are twelve for the third and fourth [dhyānas], and six for the Fourth Dhyāna: the Puṇyaprasava, Vṛhatphala, and Avṛha.
Regarding the *phala-devas* (fruition deities), the three higher ones are each distinct; these are the three grades of karma from the older tradition. Below them, there are another three:
Śuci, Īśvara, and Maheśvara. Thus, nine are established, totaling eighteen, which does not contradict the reception of the bodhisattva precepts.
Question: Although this explanation exists, does it not contradict [the established doctrine]? Answer: There are two types of heavens; Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna each speak of eighteen.
Regarding the three classes of karma-retribution heavens within each of the four dhyānas, Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna are the same.
Beyond these, if one follows the Hīnayāna system of heavens, one adds the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens and the Asaṃjñisattva heaven to constitute eighteen. These are not used here. If...
According to the Mahāyāna, one additional bodhisattva heaven is added to each of the first three dhyānas; these are collectively designated as such.
In the fourth dhyāna, three separate bodhisattva heavens are added. Why is this? Because those in the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are born in those [heavens] respectively.
As for the previously mentioned three added heavens, they are not fixed to lower stages, and thus only one is added in total, respectively.
It is taught that these eighteen Brahmā heavens exist; therefore, this statement does not contradict the fact that one receives the bodhisattva precepts there.
This is as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*. Let no one harbor doubts or slander.

Section. Regarding the statement that one "cannot separately receive the Prātimokṣa precepts": this meaning does not permit a noble one (ārya) to receive them separately. Aside from noble ones, there are those who do receive them separately;
however, since the preceding [text] speaks only of noble ones, there is no separate reception, but only a general reception.

Question: It was previously stated that even in the ten stages (daśabhūmi), there is new reception. This must be received again by one who has already [received it] before. As for that which is relinquished, is it not...?
It is not received separately; moreover, since that text states that one still relinquishes the renunciant precepts at the end of life, this implies they are received separately. Answer:

That [text] refers generally to the lower realms, whereas this treatise concerns the upper realms. Because there is no appearance of renunciation and the mind lacks extreme aversion [to cyclic existence], there is no separate reception [of the precepts].
Question: What is the meaning of "receiving [the precepts] universally"? Answer: The meaning of receiving them universally is that it does not pertain to a single lifetime;

therefore, it does not exclude rebirth in the lower realms, as one must maintain them throughout. Furthermore, when it says "excepting," this excludes the upper realms, yet they exist in the lower realms.

This implies that if ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) are permitted to receive the precepts separately while remaining householders, why would it not be permitted for noble ones (ārya) to do so? Another interpretation takes the first two lines of this passage as restating the case of ordinary persons.

There is no distinct manifestation; it applies only to sensation (*vedanā*). Furthermore, the next two phrases clarify that while noble ones (*ārya*) have distinct sensations and distinct liberations, this conversely reveals that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) lack these, though their essential point remains.

The explanation regarding the lower realms of the higher worlds clarifies the principle of the ordinary being: unlike the noble one, who does not require extreme loathing [of the lower] yet is permitted to experience [the higher], the ordinary being may either universally loathe the three realms or specifically loathe the desire realm.
As for the noble one, they universally loathe the three realms; even when loathing the desire realm, they possess [this capacity]. The ordinary being, however, loathes...
Manifesting in a body that is free from desire and similar states, because there is no extreme sense of revulsion, there is no distinct sensation (*vedanā*).

This interpretation holds that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the higher realms experience only general sensations and do not admit distinct ones; whereas for noble ones (*ārya*), both general and distinct sensations are admitted. This interpretation is slightly superior.

Prior to entering the stages (*bhūmi*), Bodhisattvas—whether lay or ordained—are unable to practice equally; however, once they have entered the stages, equal practice is permitted, and thus it is also permitted for the laity to receive [the precepts].

Regarding the household precepts (*gṛhī-śīla*): those who are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and bodhisattvas who receive them collectively do so not merely for the duration of a single lifetime; thus, their reception is permitted.

Those who receive them separately do so because they are in this present body, yet lack the appearance of one who has left the household life (*pravrajita*), or lack the sense of renunciation regarding desire; therefore, there is no separate reception [of the full monastic vows].

As for the lay follower (*upāsaka*), since they must rely upon both the lay and the monastic communities, and because they also possess renunciation regarding desire, there is likewise no [separate reception of the full vows].
Regarding this principle:
since it is already granted that those in the desire heavens and so forth [possess the precepts], one admits that ordinary persons in the desire heavens receive them separately.

This is because lay followers (*upāsaka*) and those with separate liberation possess both desire and aversion, and because they possess objective entities; furthermore, they are not renunciants. For the five groups of renunciants, the separate liberation is obtained through universal reception. [This applies to] the noble ones (*ārya*).
The rest is as before. Question: How is it that the various noble ones and bodhisattvas do not receive [rebirth]? And how can there be relinquishment throughout the limits of the future?
Answer: This has already been explained as before.
Section. Regarding "but not being of that nature": for example, although a paṇḍaka possesses those precepts, they cannot be called a lay follower (upāsaka) or a lay follower woman (upāsikā);
thus, they are said to be "not of that nature."
Therefore, there are cases of *prātimokṣa* that are not the bodhisattva precepts; such instances may exist, though they differ from those in hell.

In hell, there is no *prātimokṣa* that is not the bodhisattva *prātimokṣa* precept, because there exists only the bodhisattva *prātimokṣa* precept. After hell, [the states of] hungry ghosts and animals are the same:
there are those that are not the bodhisattva *prātimokṣa* precepts, and there are those that are the bodhisattva *prātimokṣa* precepts. Such is the explanation.
The hells are excluded, with the exception of the Avīci hell; some say this is also because of the Buddha’s majestic power. Question:

This teaching allows that all five destinies may receive the precepts, yet why are they absent from the Bodhisattva Precept Sūtra? Is it because those who are transformation-beings (nirmāṇa-puruṣa) belong to the animal realm? Answer: [It is because...]
Regarding the phrase "up to and including": another interpretation is that for those who have not yet received the precepts, there is no hell;
however, within this context, the general statement regarding going there and receiving the precepts also includes hell. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Section. Regarding the phrase "Yogācāra, etc.": A lay follower (*upāsaka*) does not accept [the precepts] at all if their intention is impaired by two conditions.

As for the second case, those who live by [changing] forms are permitted to receive those precepts; they are not called lay followers, yet there is no prohibition against animals and others receiving them.

Therefore, this is taken as proof. The term "etc. includes the hells; the direct proof regarding the hells follows, and after that, the explanation arrives. Regarding hungry ghosts, slander, and lack of contention, these include both the primary and the secondary absence [of conflict].
[This is] lost. Or it may be treated as a general textual section.

Regarding the "meditative absorption restraint" (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and so forth: those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) receive their name by association [with the lower realms], without requiring a distinct conceptualization.
"Chapters," or "a small portion," and so forth, refer to the varying degrees of the categories [of afflictions] that have been subdued and abandoned.
"The above are all equal," etc., refers to the fact that, with respect to the desires and evils, one merely treats them by distancing oneself from them.
Section. Regarding "briefly not established": since it says "briefly," it is clearly understood that [the entity] actually exists. As for the term "form-precept" (*rūpa-śīla*):
the precept of non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) is called the "form-precept," which serves to distinguish it from the non-informative [precepts] within the mental faculty.

Section. Regarding the statement, "This is provisionally named 'form' (rūpa) based on what it prevents," this serves as a general explanation of its own name and initiates a refutation of alternative views.
Since it is obtained through a provisional designation, why would it prevent [the influence of] the primary elements (mahābhūta) of other realms from creating it?
[Chapter]. "By the nature of things (*dharmatā*), meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are all capable of suppressing what is non-existent" explains the intent of the refutation.

This mention of "meditative absorption" also extends to the formless realms (*ārūpya*), as it is spoken here according to their shared characteristics and their derived names. The two subsequent lines that follow conclude the refutation, which is clear. *Jíxuán* and other texts state:

"This refutes the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) position in the *Abhidharmakośa*, which asserts that [matter] is truly produced by the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Since they [the formless beings] lack a body, [such production] does not exist."
Non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*). Since he does not admit that there is the creation [of karma] by means of a different realm, [the text says]:

"If it is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)," which refers to the afflictions abandoned through the path of seeing; the subsequent mention of "the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanāmārga*) likewise refers to the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation. This distinguishes the distant separation (*dūrabhāga*) of the antidote for these two types of afflictions.

Regarding the passage "Only the six beginning with form" (*rūpa-ṣaṭka*), this is the first interpretation: the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the four fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*)—these six collectively serve as the basis for both those who transcend the afflictions (*kleśa-samatikrama*) and those who follow the sequential path (*ānupūrvika*).

For those following the sequential path, only the first preparatory stage and the first fundamental dhyāna are the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) that act as distant countermeasures (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*) for all subsequent stages.

Section. Regarding the interpretation that "only the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) [is involved]," this is the second explanation. It maintains that one can abandon the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) throughout all nine stages (*navabhūmi*).

The term "only" (*kevalam*) serves to distinguish this from the case where one transcends the afflictions through suppression (*vibhūṣaṇa*), which involves both the abandonment of the afflictions of vision (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) across five stages; here, it refers specifically to the abandonment of the afflictions of cultivation alone, thereby spanning all nine stages.
This also consolidates the afflictions and transcends the person, encompassing the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), as was previously stated.
Regarding the passage "Sūtra says: 'one who leaps over the first fruit,' etc.": One who leaps over that which is above the first fruit is called "one who leaps over the first fruit.

Alternatively, reading the two characters separately, they briefly indicate the "bundles of afflictions" (saṃyojana). Below this, it mentions one who, from above the first fruit, directly attains the fourth; these are the two [skips] among the leap-attainers.
This person is permitted to abandon the afflictions of the desire realm based on the nine stages.

Regarding the passage "Although one knows that the treatise... and so forth: since the *Abhidharma* states that this relies solely on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage, it must be reconciled with the present context.

That treatise makes its determination based on the "distant" (*viprakṛṣṭa*) stages above; therefore, it speaks only of the stages above as being "distant," because they do not serve as antidotes [to the desire realm].
The above summary may include explanations based on the presence of antidotes that sever [defilements]. In reality, it does not preclude the existence of distant antidotes for the higher stages.

Those who changed the character "distant" (yuan) to "near" (jin) have failed to grasp the intended meaning of this treatise. The preceding masters also provided a combined interpretation, stating that it refers to the "uninterrupted" (*anāgamya*) stage;
one should know this by comparison with this point. Within the *Shuyao*, there is only the latter interpretation, which does not include the six stages.

Section: Clarifying the Meaning of Attainment and Abandonment, etc. The preceding clarifies the basis of the stages (*bhūmi*); the following clarifies the basis of the person (*āśraya*). Because they possess the quality of being "distant" (*viprakṛṣṭa*), they pertain to all three realms;
however, abandonment and the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) apply only to the desire realm.
Regarding the section on "non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*) and so forth: the body [of the argument] follows the sequence of the preceding sections.

Regarding the section on "abiding in the middle": there were previously two interpretations; the first held that it pertained only to the contaminated (*sāsrava*), while the latter held that it applied to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Although the former was correct in restricting it to the contaminated, the present text records the latter view which applies it to both. Therefore, we know that the two masters’ positions may be used in combination.
...so as not to cause [the reader] to cling [to them].
Regarding the passage "The forms of body and speech," etc.: previously, the actual manifest karma (*vijñapti-karma*) was explained in general;

here, the two types of nominal karma (*prajñapti-karma*) are explained specifically. Therefore, the text does not repeat itself. Furthermore, within the category of the intermediate [karma], this includes the untainted (*anāsrava*), as it can be subsumed therein.

This is stated from a partial perspective. As for the other two types of false [views], they are not untainted (*anāsrava*). Since this delusion extends even to the Buddha, it is said to be "untainted.

The mention of "the two realms" is a general reference; alternatively, it may be stated by including those that resemble the desire realm through transformation, or by treating them collectively because they arise due to the untainted.
