Regarding the phrase "its manifest [action] and so forth": "and so forth" includes non-manifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*). The upper portion refers to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), while the lower portion cites that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, the mention of the "three realms" in the lower portion is a general reference.

Section. Regarding the phrase "excluding the wholesome [states] of the vows (saṃvara), etc.": it should be considered that those which encompass the welfare of others through the cultivation of goodness are all intermediate [neutral states], whether they apply to the Buddha or not.
Section. Regarding the phrase "only in the human realm": this applies only to the three continents, but does not apply to the desire-realm heavens.

Section. Alternatively, it is said that [the precepts] exist in all realms except for the hells. The previous statement held that those possessing the complete precepts (*sīla*) are merely those abiding in the intermediate state;

this present statement holds that the restraint (*saṃvara*) does not extend to the hells. Thus, they are not contradictory. This constitutes one interpretation regarding the division of restraint within the *Śīla*.

The *Jíxuán* (Compendium of Mysteries) provides a general explanation of both the "existence" and "non-existence" interpretations, stating: "The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* does not mention the hells; therefore, they are excluded."
Section. Regarding the statement that "the non-restraint mind is not superior," this is because it lacks the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Section.

Regarding the reference to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*), etc., its [non-restraint] matter (*rūpa*) is associated with the meditative and the path; it does not mention what is produced [by it].

Section: Regarding those who possess the distinct liberation of the three realms, the *Jixuanjie* (Collection of Profound Explanations) states: "This includes both the meditative (*samādhi*) and the path (*mārga*) [liberations]; or alternatively, those who have produced the provisions (*sambhāra*) for them also receive it.
Section: As for the phrase "even the Buddha-body" and so forth, these all refer to the prevention of evil within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Section: To clarify and distinguish those who have attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*). This is because there are those who have not yet produced [the Path] despite having attained concentration;

thus, to distinguish them from those who have both attained concentration and produced the Path, it is stated in this manner by combining the discussion of what is prevented with its underlying causes. Therefore, it is as follows.
Section. Regarding the phrase "one who kills the people of a nation," the subsequent mention of "three nations" refers to citing a single name as representative of one;
furthermore, it carries the sense of "fulness," as in the expression "the full nation."
Section. Regarding the fact that the Hīnayāna necessarily possesses manifest action (*vijñapti*), it is explained below. The *Nyāyabindu-śāstra* (Treatise on Right Reasoning) states:
"Because of mental agitation, his body and speech necessarily undergo change; or, due to incantations and curses, his body and speech are inevitably moved."

Section. Regarding the Mahāyāna position that killing is initiated solely by the informative act (*vijñapti-karman*) of the mind: this first restates the Mahāyāna doctrine. What follows below poses a question;

it asks only about the name and the formation of matter (*rūpa*), but does not ask about the characteristics of the completed act of killing. Below, the completion of the act of killing is cited to clarify the nature of the formed matter (*rūpa*).
Section. "If it were not so" means: if it were not the case that killing occurs solely through mental formation (*manomaya*), and so forth.

That treatise clearly refers to this as "mental punishment" (*mana-daṇḍa*). The *Jixuan* commentary explains: "Punishment" (*daṇḍa*) means sin (*āpatti*). I [the present author] say: it refers to disciplinary punishment. It is the disciplinary punishment of sentient beings.

Section. Regarding the phrase "Now, as for 'equal' and so forth": the two lines of text collectively state that the accomplishment of killing also involves instrumental means (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, the following two lines also collectively address the conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), stating:
since there are both names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) in this context, and there are already the instruments of killing, there must necessarily be both form and name.

Section. Regarding the phrase "this is not the intention of that treatise," etc., the following section clearly demonstrates its specific characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). First, it shows that the treatise does not establish [the act] through the mind alone;
rather, it must involve the provisional employment of another's body and speech to effect a killing. That it now receives the name "form" (*rūpa*) is because it traces back to that [external factor].
As for the direct designation of "form" based on another's body and speech, while it is called "mind-only" (*manomātra*), there is no fault in this from the perspective of one's own [internal state].

Section: Regarding the statement that "bodily and vocal actions must necessarily have a manifest characteristic (*nimitta*)," this is a refutation by inversion. How can one explain the characteristics of the bodily and vocal movements of a non-Buddhist practitioner (*ṛṣi*) as described in the Śrāvaka schools?

Although they speak of curses (*abhiśāpa*), no such teachings are found in the scriptural canons. Question: As it is said, prior to the recitation of the precepts, if one has a transgression and does not speak of it, it constitutes a deliberate falsehood (*saṃprajāna-mṛṣāvāda*).
With reference to what *nāma-rūpa* (name-and-form) is this defined? Answer: Because of his silence, the Dharma Master knows [the assembly] is pure and issues the formal motion (*jñapti*).

Because it arises from the body and speech of a Dharma Master; furthermore, it is also performed by invoking spirits and deities through their bodies and speech, much like the intention of those ancient seers.

Another interpretation is that just as a harmful color may not necessarily be currently manifest, yet is still designated by its name, so too here, one silently takes the place of speech and says, "I am pure," thereby establishing the rite. Let us further reflect upon this explanation.
Chapter. Regarding these two explanations: the statement that there is a manifest [action] (vijñapti) which is exclusively mental constitutes the "two explanations.
Chapter. As for the phrase "therein are two": this topical division is not part of the main text; rather, it is a separate section concerning the transmission between teacher and disciple.
Section. Furthermore, regarding "being coerced and recorded": this refers to being pressured into making a formal record.

Section. Regarding "although harboring fear and so forth": this means that one might act out of fear of being expelled, thereby revealing that the practice is not genuine. Moreover, it indicates that the practice is incomplete;
because one constantly practices only a single aspect [of the path], one fears expulsion.
"Chapter. Then, regarding the phrase "those whose intentions [are thus]," the word "those" (te) refers back to the aforementioned word in the subsequent treatise;
or else, it means that because they falsely manifest themselves as inferior for their own sake, they bring about harm.

Section. Regarding the phrase "If there should be another person," etc.: this refers to the second type of person mentioned below, who is not called a "harmer. This is because they do not feign [the practice], but rather truly cultivate it.
Section. Regarding the phrase "Because they thus lack such power and ability": this merely restates the aforementioned lack of power and ability. The preceding [passage]...
The treatise states: "Although one has left the household life, one lacks the power to serve one's preceptors and elders.
Regarding the phrase "the objects received from preceptors and others," this section below cites two types of objects received; it refers to the objects received from preceptors and others.
These objects are termed the "activity of service," because they are obtained through one's own act of service. This is the activity (*karman*).
Just as with household affairs—where one's own property is called "affairs"—this [robe] likewise is not a thing given out of faith;
therefore, it is generally designated below as that which is bestowed by those of pure faith.
Regarding the passage on "receiving pure faith, practice, and so forth": the upper part refers to receiving the master's property, while the lower part refers to receiving offerings for oneself.

Following this text, it generally concludes that [the offerings] are difficult to digest; because they are difficult to digest, they cause internal conflict and exhaustion, thereby destroying the roots of goodness.
Some interpret this as the destruction of the roots of goodness resulting from the decline of faith and offerings, but this does not reach the meaning of the former [explanation].
Section. Regarding *śaṇḍha* and *paṇḍaka*: Zuǎn says, "*Śaṇḍha*" here means "one without the power of the organ" (*mūla-vaśitā*);
"*Paṇḍaka*" here means "desire" (*ruci*). This is because taking pleasure in others is considered a fault for oneself.

Section. Furthermore, regarding those such as the *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs/impotent persons), there are three types within the second category. According to the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma-piṭaka*), there are five:

those who are so from birth (*jātipaṇḍaka*), those who are so for half a month (*pakṣapaṇḍaka*), those who are so through jealousy (*īrṣyāpaṇḍaka*), those who are so by sprinkling [semen] (*sekapaṇḍaka*), and those who are so by removal (*apahāraka*). Of these, "those who are so from birth" and "those by removal" correspond respectively to the first and last [of our two categories].

As for the distinction between these two: the former refers to one who, throughout their entire life, lacks the male faculty and power, and who necessarily takes pleasure in others while considering themselves to be at fault.
The *śaṇḍha* is called a *paṇḍaka*. The third [type] previously possessed the functional power of a male organ, which later ceased to exist.
Because they do not invariably take pleasure in others, this constitutes a fault regarding themselves; thus they are either simply *śaṇḍhas* or receive both names.
Within this limited category, there are three types mentioned in this text. All three possess the functional power of a male organ and are not *śaṇḍhas*; they certainly take pleasure in others.
One who has committed this transgression is called a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch). Zuan states: "In this context, there is no mention of *abhiṣeka* (consecration/semen);
rather, it opens up 'jealousy' (*īrṣyā*) as two types: one where the male function arises in oneself toward another, and one where the male function arises in oneself toward others.
As for *abhiṣeka*, the male function arises only upon obtaining the semen and blood of another; these belong to the category of jealousy and are not [simply] termed 'jealousy'. [End of] Collection.
Xuán asked: "In this context, are those with both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana) included? He replied with two interpretations:
first, that they are included within the aforementioned category of envy (*īrṣyā*); second, that they are not included.

However, he stated that the latter explanation is correct, because the *Abhidharmapitaka* (Dàfǎ lùn) treats the *śaṇḍha* and *paṇḍaka* as examples alongside those with both sexual organs. Now, it seems necessary here to...

It is included therein; however, it is subsumed within the category of those who observe the half-month [vows] for both men and women. Herein, for the time being, those with fixed seasons are cited as a representative class for those without fixed seasons.
That text provides a separate example for those who have no fixed seasons.
Section. Regarding "heretics who dwell as thieves": Master Zhou says that a heretic who falsely assumes the guise of a bhikṣu is called one who "dwells as a thief.

If, at the time of receiving the precepts, the necessary conditions are not fulfilled, then although they have received them, they possess no precepts; yet they remain among the bhikṣus and participate in the *poṣadha* together with them.

This is also called "thieving residence" (*caura-vāsa*). The *Jixuanjie* (Exegesis on the Collection of Mysteries) states: "To falsely present oneself as a bhikṣu with the intent to seek out [others'] faults is called thieving residence.
Regarding the passage "if one dwells separately," Master Zhou says: "One who has committed a root offense and repented is called 'dwelling separately' (*pṛthag-vāsa*);
one who does not repent is called 'not dwelling together' (*asaṃvāsa*). The *Jixuanjie* further states: "One who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense is called..."
"Dwelling separately" refers to the offense of *pārājika*, which is termed "not living in communion. There are instances where *pārājika* is translated as "not living in communion.
Now, it is said that these two names refer to two distinct offenses. *Pārājika* refers to the retribution in a future life; the name of the offense is derived from its fruit.
"Non-residence" (*asaṃvāsa*) refers to disciplinary punishment in the present life; it does not allow one to participate in the *poṣadha* together with the Saṅgha.
Since this constitutes two offenses, it should not be translated as "non-residence.

Therefore, there is no "non-residence" in the Mahāyāna, because the Mahāyāna lacks such disciplinary punishments for offenses, lacks congregations [of monastics], and is common to the fourfold assembly. Laypeople do not incur this offense; thus, there is no "non-residence."
Now, regarding these rules: furthermore, this single name possesses no dual characteristics, for the conduct is identical whether one has already confessed or has not yet confessed.
Thus, the Vinaya-mūla states: "As it was before, so it shall be after. Therefore, do not divide it into two. Moreover, this explains that receiving the precepts is not permitted;

what does this have to do with those who have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense? Although they have violated the precepts, they still remain within the community; thus, there is no need [to exclude them].

Because it is received [as a formal status], one should state this: "Those who dwell separately" refers to those among the community of renunciants who are unwilling to perform their duties for half a year, or those who have never previously served as a *śrāmaṇera*.
Although they have shaved their hair and beards, because they dwell separately, they cause harm to the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) and are therefore not granted ordination.
Since they do not dwell in common, do not grant them the precepts again.
Section. Regarding "if there are kings, ministers, and so forth": based on this, one must not bestow the precepts upon them. This is because kings and ministers have mutual ties of dependency;

how could it be conceivable for them to listen to one another [in the context of ordination]? Alternatively, if a king’s minister is someone the king dislikes, he may not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If he has been plundered by others, he is captured by bandits. If he has fallen into the hands of others, he is a person without anyone to rely upon.

"Being taken in by another" means being separated from one's parents by another. Zuan says: "If a lowly person’s parents are adopted by another, although they are not their biological parents, they are nonetheless acquired by that other."
[Section] "Having already fallen asleep": "already" (ji) here refers to having awakened. The *Śāstra* says: "Having already slept and then awakened.
[Section] "If one is a garden-keeper": *Zuǎn* says this refers to the person who guards the temple gate. From this point downward is precisely the meaning of that which is to be protected.
Fearing slander of the truth, [one should know] that these are all non-humans.
Chapter. One who acquires this evil view will harbor hatred and loathing. Chapter.
Or, for the sake of receiving [the gift], if it merely harms the physical form but does not harm the intention, one may accept it; however, if it harms...
The intention [of the author] is simply not to admit [this]. Therefore, the word "or" (*vā*) is placed [in the text].

Regarding the statement in the treatise, "The causes and conditions were not mentioned [here] because they have already been fully analyzed previously": this refers to those who do not become lay followers (*upāsaka*).

This is the text of the treatise. Previously, the treatise had stated: "Question: Why is it that although these two (the *ṣaṇḍha* and the *paṇḍaka*) have received refuge, they are also able to subsequently undertake the various [precepts of a] lay follower?"
Can one who observes all the training rules of a male lay follower (*upāsaka*) not be called a male lay follower? Answer:
A male lay follower is so named because he is able to draw near to and serve the community of monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*).

Although he is able to guard the moral discipline (*vinaya*) he has received, he should not frequently draw near to and serve the community of monks and nuns; nor do the monks and nuns [require such service from him].
Furthermore, one should not associate with or embrace them through such acts as rubbing or touching.
Nor should one cultivate intimacy with them as one does with an upāsaka. Therefore, such individuals cannot be called upāsakas;
nevertheless, it should be understood that there is no difference in the merit regarding the training rules they have undertaken.

Section. It should not be for the sake of one who receives [the precepts]. There is a saying that combines this with the character "shou" (授, to bestow). Now, observing both the beginning and the end, we see it pertains to the method of providing support.
This combined character "shou" (受, to receive) should simply be pronounced with a level tone as "wei" (為, to act as). "Wei" means "to act as. It does not mean "one who receives."
Section. Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*)," the treatise explains the first three categories.

This passage is translated universally as "should receive," referring to all three categories. The treatise simply states: "It should be known that one should receive all the restraints (*saṃvara*) as previously described.

It lacks the characters *wei* (to act for/as) and *juzu* (full/complete). The addition of the character *juzu* (full ordination) serves to clarify the distinct characteristics of the three [categories]. This is illustrated by a single example.
"Remainder" (*yu*) means "still performing. It is not fit to serve as a support.
Regarding the passage "Śīla is not pure," etc., it follows from this that one must possess the complete precepts (*śīla*) in order to attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Question: But can one induce concentration simply by refraining from evil? Answer: According to this, it requires the precepts. Question: For example, when the kalpa is destroyed, one naturally attains concentration; and...

If one cultivates the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñin*), is it not preceded by the precepts? The answer is: at the beginning of a kalpa of destruction, there are also bodhisattvas and pratyekabuddhas who cause others to cultivate [it].
The ten unwholesome actions are themselves their precepts. As for the three refuges, they may already exist [prior to that], or when a Buddha is present, the three refuges are required;
even in a world where no Buddha exists, the Dharma and the Saṅgha are still available. To say "spontaneously" means that it does not require external conditions.

Furthermore, that which is called "spontaneous" (svayambhū) refers to the absence of the Buddha-dharma; it does not mean that there is no cultivation or practice. Its cultivation is characterized by non-conceptualization (asaṃjñā).

By this principle, one must first cultivate the ten wholesome precepts before attaining the first dhyāna, and so on, until one eventually gives rise to false views regarding the higher realms and cultivates the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñi-samāpatti).
It is not that one does not guard against desire and wrong views; it is simply because this volition (cetanā) is not said to be cultivated simultaneously with them.

This is because meditative concentration (samādhi), ethical discipline (śīla), and volition necessarily coexist. Thus, regarding all wholesome dharmas, if they do not first rely upon a single instance of ethical discipline and volition...
If one cannot even achieve the status of a human or deva, how much less can one attain the higher realms? When aided by ethical discipline (*śīla*), one achieves success accordingly.

Whether collectively or individually, humans and devas are honored and noble. Question: If that is so, how does one attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to prevent evil? Answer: This should be considered as previously explained.

Furthermore, depending on the case, ethical discipline prevents certain evils but need not eliminate them entirely; meditative concentration prevents those remaining. Those branches which are identical [in function] should be considered accordingly.
Furthermore, there are varying degrees of protection, depending on whether one is a *votthabba* (one who has fallen away) or a *santatinirodha* (one whose continuity has ceased), and so forth.
Regarding the statement in the chapter that "it is not necessary to receive the precepts again": Question: Since the secondary rules (*aṅga*) for nuns are numerous, how can they be obtained?

Answer: Those that differ are merely the points of training (*śikṣāpada*). Since there is no difference in the fundamental precepts (*mūla-śīla*) that have been received, one does not receive them again. One receives [them once].
Because the factors of fulfillment consist solely of the fundamental [vows]. That which differs is the factor of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*). Question:
When a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) undergoes a sex change, why must they receive the six rules again? Answer: Because it requires two years; because receiving the six rules is distinct from being a novice;
and because the method of receiving them is the same for both monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*).
Section: "Furthermore, adding one more" means that according to the *Ji xuanye* (Collection of Profound Explanations), this is based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, there is the addition of "not eating at improper times. If one speaks of the six rules according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, the four grave offenses constitute the first four;
the fifth is not to come into physical contact with a male, meaning above the wrist; the sixth is not to grasp the hand of a male, meaning [the act of] releasing [the grip].
Below this, the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* further states: "The six rules are: first, one must not travel alone on a road;
second, one must not cross a river alone; third, one must not touch the body of a man;
fourth, one must not sleep in the same room as a male; fifth, one must not act as a matchmaker for marriages; sixth, one must not..."

Regarding the grave offense of concealing [a nun's transgression], both the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* state that ordination is received through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations).

If the *Mūla-sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states that it is received through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), these various vinayas differ according to their respective schools.

As for the statement in the previous chapter that one obtains the six precepts at the conclusion of the Three Refuges, this is explained from the perspective of the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇerikā*, as there is no separate set of precepts other than those very ones.
Therefore, if explained individually, it is in fact obtained at the conclusion of the *karmavācanā*. Or, it may be a single school;
if two schools differ, their methods of receiving the precepts are identical.

Section. Regarding those who follow the five precepts and so forth: because the methods of receiving them differ, they must be received again. When monks and nuns convert from one another’s status, the method of receiving the precepts does not differ;

it is only the points of training (*śikṣāpada*) that differ, and thus they do not receive them again. Although these are received repeatedly, they do not constitute a separate perfuming (*vāsana*), as they share the same basis for the precepts.

The precepts perfumed when a *śrāmaṇera* receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) serve as the basis [for subsequent stages]. However, Master Xuansheng states that these are merely prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepa-śīla*).

This refers to that which is added. By this standard, when a *bhikṣuṇī* receives the six rules of training (*ṣaḍ-dharmāḥ*), whether through a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*) or two proclamations (*jñapti-dvitīya*), it is likewise merely an addition of conditions.
When a *śrāmaṇera* receives full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), what is added pertains to the universal nature [of the precepts].

Section. Regarding "if one firmly undertakes [the precepts] through speech and so forth," this does not refer to the three clusters [of pure conduct]. One receives all seven clusters of pure conduct simultaneously.
Section. Regarding "if one speaks of them horizontally," the five groups of renunciants do not include those who dwell in the middle [lay practitioners].

Section. Regarding the phrase "at the time of relinquishing," etc., this serves to clarify the opposite case. The following is the actual text: when the roots of goodness are severed or at the end of life, one definitely and simultaneously relinquishes them;
however, regarding the transgression of vows, it is not fixed.
Section. Regarding the term "upāsaka" and so forth, the term "saka" is to be understood accordingly.

For the two groups of householders, as well as those who practice the middle way in its entirety or gradually, the Vinaya distinguishes between gradual and middle-way practitioners, both of which are explained as previously stated.

Section. Furthermore, regarding the statement "the five hundred precepts for bhikṣuṇīs" and so forth: this question concerns whether a bhikṣuṇī who has converted to become a formal student (śaikṣa) should abandon or not abandon [the bhikṣuṇī precepts].
Although it is stated generally that there are seven points, the intent actually lies in four branches. Whether they are to be abandoned or not abandoned.
Section. Regarding the phrase "one says, etc.": the second explanation below is identical to the previous one, whereas this first explanation differs from the previous one.
It merely omits the three branches of the complete precepts (*upasampadā*), while not omitting the four branches common to both. Question: For what reason are they not the same?

Furthermore, the reasoning presented here directly contradicts the previous reasoning, which stated that the essence [of the precepts] is the same in that all are abandoned. This [second explanation]...

[Question: Regarding the principle that they are identical in essence and not abandoned, [the opponent] asks: "This [statement] refers only to the abandonment of the *śikṣāpada* (precepts of training) associated with the *dhyāna-saṃvara* (meditative discipline), yet it is made as a question regarding the non-abandonment of the *śaikṣa-dharma* (precepts of those in training).
Since it has already been stated that the precepts of one in training are not abandoned, how can these four be abandoned in the same manner as those?

[The Master replies: The preceding discussion concerned the general characteristics. [Question: Since abandoning and not abandoning are of the same essence, they should all be abandoned at once. As for the preceding...
Regarding those that are identical in substance, they are all abandoned simultaneously; regarding those identical in substance, they are likewise not abandoned.

Therefore, it is said they "properly conform. This is the second explanation below: although the four are identical in substance, since their characteristics are distinct, one also abandons all seven, because the four of the *śikṣamāṇā* still remain.

Based on this, it appears that when the basis for the recitation of the precepts differs, the preceding and succeeding cases are treated analogously; thus, even if the names are the same, it is permissible [to apply the rule]. However—
This must be further considered. Question: If, when previously asked about relinquishing the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts, one does not mention the ten precepts, how is this to be explained?
Answer: There is no reason for relinquishing six [precepts] rather than ten, because there is no distinction at all; it is not like the seven branches, which separately have three [aspects].
Question: If one asks only about relinquishing what has been added, how is that? Answer: Apart from the four, asking in this way is likewise not prohibited. This...

Regarding the abandonment through formal renunciation (*samādāna-tyāga*): because it is performed according to one’s capacity, and because the preceding inquiry concerned only the substance of the four branches, the answer was given categorically as being complete in six factors—since the three branches, when fully understood, constitute these six factors. Thus, this may be posed as a question and answered in two ways; this must be reflected upon. Question:

How does one abandon [the precepts] through transgression? Answer: It must necessarily be simultaneous, including the five precepts and so forth. This is the explanation of Master Zhou; it has been compiled here.

Xuán also understands this, stating that both [the full ordination and the novice vows] consist of the complete performance of the six dharmas; they differ in that the four branches [of the full ordination] involve relinquishment, whereas the six dharmas do not.

He claims there is no difference in the method for receiving the novice dharma, asserting that it must necessarily involve simultaneous relinquishment. Now, I say that one must reflect upon whether the methods of receiving these dharmas are identical or distinct.

Furthermore, if one dies or commits a grave offense, it must be immediate. Someone has raised this question: "How is it that at the time of receiving [the precepts], one must immediately [perform the three...]"?

Next, regarding the time of relinquishment, there is likewise a simultaneous [relinquishment]. Answer: The difficulty and ease differ; this can be considered by analogy with ascending or descending a mountain.
Now, it is explained that at the time of receiving [the precepts], there is also a simultaneous [receiving], as in the case of the Threefold Aggregate Precepts (*tri-skandhaka-śīla*).

This is because the Śrāvakas have small power and narrow capacity, and thus their [practice] is necessarily gradual. Question: What is the nature of first receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and subsequently receiving the Threefold Aggregate Precepts? Answer:

Just as one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) through six factors, here [in the bodhisattva vow] one merely adds the three mental actions and includes the "gathering of wholesome qualities" (*kuśaladharmasaṃgraha*), while the remaining [factors] only increase the objects of focus.
All precepts that ought to be observed likewise extend to the end of the future, because they are augmented by the assistance of repeated vows. Question:

What is meant by "one who has regressed from the bodhicitta and abandoned it"? Answer: One who has regressed and returned to the two vehicles retains the śrāvaka precepts; one who has regressed and returned to the non-Buddhists [retains] all [of their precepts].
All are absent; one should reflect upon this with thorough scrutiny.

Regarding the chapter on "Transgressing the Heavy [Precepts] and Abandoning [the Path]," which states "as in returning to external paths," the commentary explains that cultivation resides in the present, or the fruit returns to the seed;
all cases are like this, because the seeds bring about the completion of present actions.

Section. Regarding the phrase "by these [factors]": they receive their name by following from their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). To dispel lingering doubts, it is provisionally designated as "not this" (*na-idaṃ*); thus there is no fault.

It follows the mind, belongs to the family of the mind, is perfumed by the family of the mind, and brings about the fruit of the habitual karma (*vāsanā-karma*) belonging to the family of the mind, because they are in a state of mutual necessity.

This refers specifically to the arising [of the fruit] from the seed alone; however, if one speaks generally of "bringing about," then "inducing" is what is meant by "bringing about," and this also applies to the manifest (*dṛṣṭadharma*).

[Objection: No, it is not so. What would be the use of practicing [the path] in the present? [Question: How is the morality of the path (mārga-śīla) defined? [Answer: It is explained in terms of the support (*upadhi*), namely, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Regarding the phrase "one version says 'and so forth,'" this is a teaching of the Hīnayāna; it claims that even sages move their lips and mouths [when speaking].
Since there is no scriptural authority for this, it cannot be relied upon as evidence.

Section. Regarding the phrase "for instance, etc.," this raises various explanations concerning the gravity [of the offense]. However, what is essential is the gravity of the intention (*manas*). Now, since this seer has already returned to [the realm of] body and speech, why is it called "gravity of intention"?
It is because the preceding [text] spoke only of moving the lips and mouth and so forth, which merely concludes the refutation regarding the body.
If one had previously cited [examples such as] "cursing" and so on, it would have been appropriate to conclude the refutation regarding speech.
Section. Regarding the phrase "merely by means of the sages and so forth," the following explains the general meaning.

As for the phrase "if it were thus," this section serves to restate what was previously set aside; it joins the conclusion of the objection by asking: "How can it be designated as 'unmanifest form' (*avijñapti-rūpa*)?
For it would merely be a case of [the definition] being inconsistent with the actual state. Thus, the three types of unmanifest form belonging to the mind do not need to be [discussed further].
Regarding body and speech: the answer below directly concerns their remote dependence on the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of another, as has already been explained previously. Question:

Why not simply negate them as being like non-greed and so forth, rather than stating that they depend remotely on the body and speech of another? Answer: This must be traced back to the offense of killing.
Because it is subsumed under the category of the form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*), it does not agree with the three [other] chapters.
Regarding the gravity and lightness within this: the four grave offenses (*caturguru*) are as previously stated, while the remaining are light. The seven branches are as usual.

Within two years, one must first inform [the candidate] so that they develop a sense of love and joy for it before bestowing it; this is not the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts, because the seven branches have already been received.

[This is] a contradiction. Regarding the "Chapter" (zhāng), the question "For what reason... and so forth asks about those items added above the eight; the subsequent question regarding the "eight combined" asks about those opened up from this [set].

The phrase "separated from money" (lí qián) means "separation" (lí) in the sense of being far removed. Together with the following, these constitute the additions above the eight; among the eight [categories],...

Because this [distinction] does not exist, it is raised as a question. As for the phrase "generated image" (*jǐngxiàng*), it refers to the image of sentient beings (*zhòngshēng*). There is another interpretation: one might doubt this and cite it briefly;
in that view, "generated" (*shēng*) refers to gold, while "image" (*xiàng*) refers to silver.
Chapter. Regarding the question "Why, etc.": As for these eight precepts, they consist of the five precepts with three additional ones: one must not sit or lie upon high, wide, or large beds;
one must not intentionally go to watch or listen to singing, dancing, or musical performances; and one must not anoint the body with fragrant oils.
One does not eat at improper times. Regarding the ten precepts for a śrāmaṇera: in addition to these eight, one adds the previous prohibition against handling gold, silver, and so forth.

This [prohibition] is waived when going to witness or listen to singing, dancing, or musical performances, which constitutes one [offense]; and applying fragrant oil to the body constitutes another. "Leaving" (li) means to permit.

Because [such acts] invite public censure, they are permitted only as exceptions; this demonstrates that what is essential must be firm. It is not the case that all [rules] are treated in this manner.

Chapter. Regarding the question concerning the universal reception of the bodhisattva precepts and so forth: according to the intent of this question, receiving the threefold aggregate precepts (tri-skandhaka-śīla) also entails receiving the precepts of meditative concentration (samādhi) and the path (mārga), as these are determined by the specific period of commitment.
Section. Regarding the passage, "If a bodhisattva gives rise to a divergent mind," etc.: since this is termed "abandonment," it should be termed a "deficiency" and should be termed "lack of precepts.

How, then, can it be called being "endowed with the morality that accords with the mind"? It cannot be said that [this endowment] lasts until the end of the future; such is the intent of this question.
Section. Answer: Because the seeds exist within the body. To possess those seeds is also called "possessing. These seeds are not inherently existing (*prakṛtistha*) seeds;
they are newly cultivated. Regarding the second explanation below: that which is capable of arising is called "possessing," and is not called "lacking" or "lost," and so forth.
Some say: because the Bodhisattva universally receives and attains both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*), he possesses them.

The seeds and those that are yet to be accomplished are not analogous to other cases; these are also the seeds of volition (*cetanā*). When discussing the time of their reception, they are all received simultaneously.

One should consider the intent of the question: what is being asked regarding "having already relinquished"? Question: Within the three aggregates, under which category are the meditative (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*) [vows] subsumed?

Answer: Because they are termed "restraints" (*saṃvara*), they are included within the category of restraint. Regarding restraint, while it is said there are seven classes of persons, in principle there are ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala*).

As for the path of meditative concentration (*samādhi-mārga*), the *upavāsa* (near-abiding) precepts pertain to both lay practitioners (*upāsaka*) and others, as they observe these eight precepts for six days out of every seven.
Regarding the statement "the five strips are always maintained;
the merit remains," etc., this concludes the response: once cultivated, they are not non-existent; those who relinquish them should be understood according to this principle. This...

Even if there were a function for the preservation of what has been cultivated, it would not be so. If [the action] is not entirely relinquished, how could there be non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)?

Although it does not possess the function of directly inducing a fruit, the seeds of its power induce the fruit. These seeds that induce the fruit may be identical to or different from [the original action];
however, the seeds that induce the fruit are more numerous than the non-informative matter itself, because non-informative matter is merely the movement and initiation of volition (*cetanā*).
Regarding the two interpretations provided in the response: according to the *Dīpa*, the first interpretation discussed in the preceding passage is the "middle way.

Furthermore, there is a third interpretation—that neither understanding nor non-understanding arises—because this [text] concerns both discipline (*vinaya*) and non-discipline (*avinaya*). Thus, there are only two interpretations; since it is impossible for one who is well-disciplined to be said to lack understanding, [the third case is excluded].

Regarding the passage, "The answer states that 'manifestation' (*vijñapti*) is itself provisional," the *Jixuan* commentary explains: "Yuan [Daoxuan] states that even the actual mind is called 'manifestation.
Regarding the passage, "'A single moment' (*kṣaṇa*) is what evokes [the result]," the character "evokes" (*gan*) is a variant for the character "extinguishes" (*mie*).
"Because it is of that same category. This refers to what was stated previously: "it receives its name from the present [state]. Question:

If that is so, why is it specifically called "conforming to the mind" (*anuparivartin*)? Answer: According to the *Zuǎn* (Compendium), it is like the Prātimokṣa vows, which, from the moment they are received, increase and develop moment by moment.

Even when encountering conditions that cause them to be relinquished, the original seeds are not destroyed; this is unlike the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), where [the vows] are said to be "abandoned" [upon their cessation].
It is relinquished. However, when the seven factors do not arise in a new moment, this is called "relinquishing the precepts.

During the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the supramundane paths (*mārga*), while one naturally possesses a mind, the seven factors increase moment by moment and multiply. If one is in a state of non-conceptualization (*acittaka*) for a certain duration, they arise as a continuity of seeds;
since there is no sense of new addition, it is termed "relinquishment. This is not like the *prātimokṣa*, which, once received, [remains] whether one has a mind or not.
The mind attains growth in all respects; therefore, it is called "conforming to the mind" (sui-xin).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Question: As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*," etc., this question and answer occurs within the section on "Acquisition and Relinquishment" (*pratilambha-prahāṇa*); its great meaning is no different [from what has been explained previously].
Following this principle, the character "man" (慢) preceding [the other] is the character "man. "Man" means "broad" (寬). The character "man" has already been explained;
I do not know for what reason or on what basis this question and answer are being repeated.

Chapter. Regarding the phrase "if one separately receives [the precepts]," etc.: those who have separately received the precepts for going forth (pravrajyā) prior to the stages (bhūmi) possess them across five categories; upon entering the stage of seeing (darśana-mārga), they possess only two;
together with the two categories of householders, there is one category in the ten stages (daśabhūmi), because of the female body of a celestial maiden (*devī*).

In this regard, according to the respective types, such receiving and relinquishing actually occurs as it is. This is because even acts such as killing are practiced in accordance with reality. Question: If that is so, why does this not apply to all seven classes of practitioners (*saptasaṃgha*)? Answer: This should be considered. This...

Regarding those who share the same precepts as the three groups (*tripuñja*), they certainly do not abandon them; whereas among these [others], there are both those who abandon and those who do not, depending on the time for which they were invited [to take the vows].

As for the interpretation in the *Ji xuanyi* (集玄義) that "those who receive [the precepts] with a mind seeking self-benefit are called 'distinct recipients' (*biéshòu*)": this statement is highly incorrect.

One should simply state: "The distinct recipients are the seven classes of followers (*saptānupūrvika*)," and within the three groups, the term "seven classes" applies universally to all who receive [the precepts].
This is for the sake of general reception.
In this chapter, it may also be said that [non-informative action] does not arise from informative action (*vijñapti*). Its arising does not depend on informative action;

its manifestation of form in relation to others is as previously explained. Mental informative action can produce bodily and vocal [informative action], and non-informative action is precisely this. Furthermore, as cited previously from the *Za lun* (Compendium), there is also...
Regarding the phrase "moving the body to cause [others] to understand" and so forth, the verbal indications of the body may all be understood by analogy.

In the Chapter, it asks: "Now, regarding the ten paths of action... As for the distinction between the non-informative (avijñapti) aspects of the paths of action, there are two types: the real seed and the provisional function; these two are not the same.

Furthermore, there are cases where there is karma but no non-informative aspect; although such a provisional [action] does not produce a result, it nonetheless arises through the power of cultivation.

Furthermore, there are those who maintain that even from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), non-informative action (*avijñapti*) can induce a fruit. The *Yideng* (The Lamp of Meaning) further states:

"If there were no distinction between non-informative action and the path of action (*karmapatha*), then non-informative action, being like [informative] action, should be subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Since their categories of inclusion are distinct, this clarifies the difference between the conventional (*prajñapti*) and the real (*dravya*)."

Furthermore, there is another explanation which states that karma is the "perfuming of the existence-part" (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*), and this is also termed "provisional" because it is established as a distinct category.
Regarding the passage, "Since in the Mahāyāna there is no [such thing]," etc., the preceding section establishes the principle, while the following section concludes the inquiry.

As for the question, "How can it arise from another if both are not 'name-and-form' (*nāmarūpa*)?", the text of the chapter provides no explicit answer; however, the intended meaning is already as explained previously. Since it is merely a provisional designation of "name-and-form," what contradiction is there in saying so?
Section. Regarding the phrase "there is no lack of [the state] of attaining Buddhahood in the present," Master Zhou said:

"This reading should be corrected; one must consult other versions. For now, I shall explain it according to its meaning. The three characters 'attaining Buddhahood' (chengfo you) are connected to what precedes them.

The subsequent four characters, 'should be from another,' refer to the present state of not abandoning [the vows]. This is connected to what follows as a challenge: how could one receive them again? The character 'yu' (with) means 'and' or 'together.'"
Furthermore, advancing to the second difficulty, it is called "giving. Regarding the passage, "How could there be naturalness if there was previously no relinquishing?

and the statement, "Obtaining the superior and relinquishing the inferior," etc., these words are specifically spoken because the fruit has just been attained. If one discusses new production, this is the case in every moment.
For this reason, the previous section refuted the Small Vehicle’s notion of "natural acquisition" (svabhāva-prāpti); ultimately, it is merely a conventional designation.

It is called "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*). Furthermore, it may be designated as such in reference to one who has abandoned the outflows (*āsrava*) and newly attained the untainted (*anāsrava*), which distinguishes it from the causal stage;
for that causal stage is not fixed, as it may also be untainted. A question is raised: "Since it is said to be spontaneous, how can it be 'received' (*vedita*)?

The answer is that it is so called by way of remote derivation. Now, the term "spontaneous" is also used to mean "received," because it is experienced without depending on the performance of a formal act.
Section. Question: "As in the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*). This refers to a wholesome mind of preparatory application, which is not a mind acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).

Section. Answer: "Wholesome or unwholesome minds of preparatory application depend upon those acquired by birth. This indicates that the minds acquired by birth exist prior [to the preparatory minds].

All [minds] acquired by birth exist first, and they are relinquished later. It is like a mass of flesh: the mind first takes recourse in it and later abandons it. Below the character for "later" (後), the preparatory [mind] is indicated.

The mind that practices [unwholesome deeds] abandons the precepts it has received and dwells in wrong views; the application of effort (prayoga) is the very act of severing the application of wholesome roots.
Alternatively, the subsequent character may be connected to the preceding one. Next, by generating the following, the characteristics are shown and explained as an analytical discernment:

at this time, one has already transgressed the previously mentioned wholesome application. "Flipping" (fan) means to transgress. "Superior" (sheng) means that even if [the wholesome roots] have been established, they are easily severed. This is...
Therefore, at the very moment one intends to sever the roots of goodness, the preparatory discipline (*prayoga-śīla*) has already been abandoned.

Because these wrong views consist of nine grades, they sever the nine grades of wholesome states of mind in reverse order; only when the highest-grade wrong view arises can it sever the lowest-grade wholesome state of mind.
Consequently, those who do not kill mosquitoes, fleas, and the like are few, and those among humans who do not kill are likewise few.
The *Biao wubiao zhang qiwan ji* (Record of Dwelling in and Delighting in the Manifest and Unmanifest) [concludes].
At this time, on the twenty-third day of the tenth month of the fifth year of Zhengde (Yimwei), the interlinear punctuation was completed.

The characters of the original manuscript were disordered; even when having others transcribe it, errors and redundancies occurred, making it difficult to understand in many places. Fortunately, I obtained a fine [copy] once again.
This should have been corrected.
